title: Ceph File System
content:
The Ceph File System interface creates virtual file systems and stores them as a series
of objects within pools. Ceph assigns these objects to placement groups and distributes or places
them pseudo-randomly in OSDs throughout the cluster.

Typically, the Ceph File System uses two pools:

- **Metadata:** The metadata pool stores the data of the Ceph Metadata Server (MDS), which
generally consists of inodes; that is, the file ownership, permissions, creation date and time, last
modified or accessed date and time, parent directory, and so on.
- **Data:** The data pool stores file data. Ceph may store a file as one or more objects,
typically representing smaller chunks of file data such as extents.

Depending upon the application consuming the Ceph File System interface, usually OpenStack
Platform, users may create, modify, and delete files in a Ceph File System. Ceph handles the create,
retrieve, update, and delete operations of each individual object representing the file.

Deleting files destroys the corresponding objects in an unrecoverable manner. However, residual
data artifacts may continue to reside on storage media until overwritten. Data may also remain in
backup archives.
section_path: Ceph File System

title: Ceph File System
content:
Ceph File System (CephFS) is a distributed file system that integrates seamlessly with
the Ceph storage architecture. By leveraging the Ceph RADOS (Reliable Autonomic Distributed Object
Store), CephFS provides a scalable and robust file system interface, adhering to POSIX standards.

Figure 1 illustrates integration of Ceph within the Ceph cluster.

Figure 1. Ceph Cluster Integration

CephFS-based file sharing offers the same desirable features as other storage services on the
Ceph platform, including scalability, high availability, and operational efficiency. The following
are key Ceph components that enable CephFS to achieve these benefits:

Object Storage Daemons (OSDs)
OSDs are responsible for storing the actual file data in CephFS. Files and directories are
represented as objects within RADOS, with OSDs managing data storage, retrieval, and replication to
ensure durability and availability. 
Ceph Monitors (MONs)
  MONs maintain the cluster map and monitor the health of the Ceph cluster. They track the state
of OSDs and other components, ensuring operational stability and fault tolerance. For CephFS, MONs
facilitate the mapping of file system operations to the underlying object storage.
Ceph Managers (MGRs)
MGRs handle cluster management, monitoring, and administrative tasks. They provide an interface
for managing the Ceph cluster and integrate with external services like OpenStack Manila and
Kubernetes CSI for additional functionalities. 
Ceph Metadata Servers (MDSs)
MDSs manage Ceph FS metadata, including file and directory operations, access control, and
namespace organization. They coordinate with OSDs to ensure consistent and efficient metadata
operations. 
Scalability
CephFS scales horizontally with the Ceph cluster, allowing for the addition of OSDs, MONs, and
MDSs to increase storage capacity and performance, accommodating large data volumes and high client
request rates.
Fault tolerance
Inheriting Ceph fault tolerance, CephFS ensures data durability and availability through
replication and erasure coding provided by RADOS, even in the event of hardware failures. 
Unified storage platform
 CephFS integrates with other Ceph storage services such as block storage, object storage,
offering a unified platform that simplifies management and supports diverse storage needs.
section_path: Ceph File System

title: Use cases for CephFS
content:
CephFS supports a range of use cases, demonstrating its scalability and flexibility to meet
various storage needs. These include: 
NFS and SMB file sharing
Clients and applications can mount and use CephFS based fileshares via the NFS or alternatively
through the SMB protocol (currently available in Technology Preview).
Native CephFS clients
Clients can mount CephFS shares directly using the kernel client (kcephfs) or FUSE (ceph-fuse),
benefiting from Ceph’s high throughput and low latency.
Kubernetes storage
CephFS can serve as backend storage for Kubernetes via the Container Storage Interface (CSI)
driver, facilitating dynamic provisioning and management of volumes for containerized applications.
section_path: Ceph File System > Use cases for CephFS

title: NFS file services
content:
Ceph NFS File Services are based on the NFS-Ganesha open-source user-space Network File
system (NFS) server that allows the export file systems using the NFS protocol. These NFS File
Services provide a highly available, high-performance and scalable solution for sharing files across
different systems in a distributed environment.

NFS can be used with either CephFS or Ceph Object Storage.
section_path: NFS file services

title: NFS with CephFS
content:
Ceph File System (CephFS) is a distributed file system designed to provide reliable and
scalable storage for large-scale deployments. It is part of the IBM Storage Ceph software-defined storage platform and offers features
like data replication, fault tolerance, and scalability. When NFS-Ganesha is used with CephFS, it
enables clients to access CephFS file systems using the NFS protocol.

Ceph NFS service gateway shows how NFS service
integrates with IBM Storage Ceph and CephFS.

Figure 1. Ceph NFS service gateway

CephFS namespaces can be exported over the NFS protocol using the NFS service NFS server with
`ceph nfs` commands.

For more information, see Exporting Ceph File System namespaces over the NFS protocol.

For more information about using the Ceph orchestrator with Cephadm in the backend to deploy the
NFS-Ganesha gateway, see Managing the NFS-Ganesha gateway using the Ceph orchestrator.
section_path: NFS with CephFS

title: NFS with Ceph Object Storage
content:
The NFS service is deployed with Ceph Object Storage backend using Cephadm. The
configuration for NFS is stored in the `nfs-pool` pool and exports are managed via
the Command-Line-interface (CLI) commands and through the Ceph dashboard.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 NFS with the Ceph Object Storage backend is not a comprehensive NFS service.
Its primary purpose is to assist in the seamless migration of legacy applications that use file to
object storage with Ceph object storage by ingesting data through NFS file systems. The data is
subsequently accessible through the S3 endpoint as an S3 bucket. For a complete NFS solution with
features such as high availability and transparent failover, you should use NFS with CephFS
backend.

For more information, see:
- Deploying NFS service with Ceph Object Storage backend
- Exporting the namespace to NFS service
- Managing NFS service exports

Ceph Object Gateway namespaces can be exported over the file-based NFSv4 protocols, alongside
traditional HTTP access protocols (S3 and Swift). In particular, the Ceph Object Gateway can now be
configured to provide file-based access when embedded in the NFS service NFS server.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Only the NFSv4 protocol is supported when using a Cephadm-based or Rook-based
deployment.
section_path: NFS with Ceph Object Storage

title: Namespace conventions
content:
NFS conforms to Amazon Web Services (AWS) hierarchical namespace conventions which map UNIX-style
path names onto S3 buckets and objects.

The top-level of the attached namespace consists of S3 buckets, represented as NFS directories.
Files and directories, subordinate to buckets, are each represented as objects, following S3 prefix,
and delimiter conventions. `/` is the only supported path delimiter.

For example, if an NFS client has mounted an RGW namespace at `/nfs`, then a file
`/nfs/mybucket/www/index.html` in the NFS namespace corresponds to an RGW object
`www/index.html` in a bucket/container `mybucket`.
section_path: NFS with Ceph Object Storage > Namespace conventions

title: Limitations on supported operations
content:
The Ceph Object Storage NFS interface supports most operations on files and directories, with the
following restrictions:

- Links, including symlinks, are not supported.
- NFS ACLs are not supported.
- Unix user and group ownership and permissions *are* supported.
- Directories may not be moved/renamed.
- Files may be moved between directories.
- Only full, sequential *write* I/O is supported
- Write operations are constrained to be uploads.
- Many typical I/O operations, such as editing files in place will fail as they perform
non-sequential stores.
- Some file utilities writing sequentially, for example, some versions of GNU tar, may fail due to
infrequent non-sequential stores.
- When mounting via NFS, sequential application I/O can generally be constrained to be written
sequentially to the NFS server via a synchronous mount option. For example, `-osync`
in Linux.
- NFS clients which cannot mount synchronously, for example, MS Windows, will not be able to
upload files.
section_path: NFS with Ceph Object Storage > Limitations on supported operations

title: Reference
content:
For more information on NFS with Ceph Object Storage, see the following:

- Creating indexless buckets
- Colocating Ceph daemons and its advantages
section_path: NFS with Ceph Object Storage > Reference

title: SMB file services
content:
You can access CephFS using the SMB protocol through the Samba suite and samba-container images that are managed by Ceph. The SMB manager module provides an interface for deploying and controlling clusters of Samba services and managing SMB shares.

With the SMB module, a cluster acts as a logical management unit that corresponds to one or more managed Samba services. A cluster can implement high-availability mechanisms or operate without them.

CephFS provides two types of management commands for SMB.
 
Imperative commands
Imperative commands provide direct instructions to create, print, or remove SMB clusters and shares. These commands allow users to manage resources through explicit commands.
Declarative commands
Declarative commands enable users to define and apply resource configurations in JSON or YAML format, allowing for consistent management of SMB clusters and shares.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Ceph managed Samba supports only SMB2 and SMB3 versions of the protocol. SMB1 (CIFS) is not supported.

For more information about SMB protocol on CephFS see, SMB protocol on Ceph File Systems.
section_path: SMB file services

title: MDS Memory Cache Limit
content:
MDS servers keep their metadata in a separate storage pool, named
`cephfs_metadata` and are the users of Ceph OSDs.

For Ceph File Systems, MDS servers support an entire IBM Storage Ceph cluster, not just a single storage device within the
storage cluster. As a result, their memory requirements can be significant. This is the case
particularly if the workload consists of small to medium-size files, where the ratio of metadata to
data is higher.

For example, to set the `mds_cache_memory_limit` to 2000000000 bytes,
run:
```bash
ceph_conf_overrides:
 mds:
 mds_cache_memory_limit=2000000000
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For a large IBM Storage Ceph cluster with a
metadata-intensive workload, do not put an MDS server on the same node as other memory-intensive
services. Doing so gives you the option to allocate more memory to MDS, for example, sizes greater
than 100 GB.

For more information, see Metadata Server
cache size limits.
section_path: MDS Memory Cache Limit

title: Benchmarking CephFS performance
content: Benchmark Ceph File System (CephFS) performance with the FIO tool.
section_path: Benchmarking CephFS performance

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Root-level access to the node.
- FIO tool is installed on the nodes.
- Block Device or the Ceph File System mounted on the node.
section_path: Benchmarking CephFS performance > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
You can use the FIO tool to benchmark Ceph File System (CephFS) performance. This tool can also
be used to benchmark Ceph Block Device.
section_path: Benchmarking CephFS performance > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Navigate to the node or the application where the Block Device or the CephFS is
mounted.

```
[root@host01 ~]# cd /mnt/ceph-block-device
 [root@host01 ~]# cd /mnt/ceph-file-system
```
2. Run FIO command. Start the `bs` value from 4k and repeat in power of 2
increments (4k, 8k, 16k, 32k ... 128k... 512k, 1 m, 2 m, 4 m) and with different
`iodepth` settings. Also run tests at your expected workload operation
size.For example, 4 K tests with different `iodepth`
values:
```
fio --name=randwrite --rw=randwrite --direct=1 --ioengine=libaio --bs=4k --iodepth=32 --size=5G --runtime=60 --group_reporting=1
```
For
example, 8 K tests with different `iodepth`
values:
```
fio --name=randwrite --rw=randwrite --direct=1 --ioengine=libaio --bs=8k --iodepth=32 --size=5G --runtime=60 --group_reporting=1
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For more information on the usage of `fio` command, see the
`fio` man page.
section_path: Benchmarking CephFS performance > Procedure

title: Managing the MDS service using the Ceph Orchestrator
content:
Use the Ceph Orchestrator with Cephadm in the backend to deploy the MDS
service.

By default, a Ceph File System (CephFS) uses only one active MDS daemon. However, systems with
many clients benefit from multiple active MDS daemons.

When managing the MDS service by using the Ceph Orchestrator, be sure to have:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Root-level access to all the nodes.
- Hosts added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor, and OSD daemons deployed.
section_path: Managing the MDS service using the Ceph Orchestrator

title: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface
content:
Using the Ceph Orchestrator, you can deploy the Metadata Server (MDS) service by using
the `placement` specification in the command-line interface.
section_path: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor, and OSD daemons deployed.
section_path: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Ceph File System (CephFS) requires one or more MDS.
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Ensure that you have at least two pools,
one for Ceph file system (CephFS) data and one for CephFS metadata.
For more information about
creating Ceph File Systems, see Creating Ceph File Systems.
To deploy the MDS service with the command-line interface, log in to the Cephadm
shell.
```bash
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
Use one of the following options to
deploy MDS daemons using placement specification.
section_path: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Use ceph fs volume to create the MDS daemons.Creating the
MDS daemons creates the CephFS volume and pools associated with the CephFS, and also starts the MDS
service on the
hosts.
```bash
ceph fs volume create FILESYSTEM_NAME --placement="NUMBER_OF_DAEMONS HOST_NAME_1 HOST_NAME_2 HOST_NAME_3"
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 By default, replicated pools are created for this command.

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs volume create test --placement="2 host01 host02"
```
section_path: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface > Procedure

title: Creating the pools, CephFS, and then deploying MDS service using placement
content: specification
section_path: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface > Creating the pools, CephFS, and then deploying MDS service using placement

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create the pools for CephFS.

```bash
ceph osd pool create DATA_POOL PG_NUM
ceph osd pool create METADATA_POOL PG_NUM
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool create cephfs_data 64
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool create cephfs_metadata 64
```
2. Create the file system for the data pools and metadata pools.

```bash
ceph fs new FILESYSTEM_NAME METADATA_POOL DATA_POOL
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs new test cephfs_metadata cephfs_data
```
3. Deploy MDS service using the ceph orch apply command.

```bash
ceph orch apply mds FILESYSTEM_NAME --placement="NUMBER_OF_DAEMONS HOST_NAME_1 HOST_NAME_2 HOST_NAME_3"
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch apply mds test --placement="2 host01 host02"
```
section_path: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface > Procedure

title: Procedure
content:
1. List the service.For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls
```
2. Check the CephFS status.For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs ls
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs status
```
3. List the hosts, daemons, and processes.

```bash
ceph orch ps --daemon_type=DAEMON_NAME
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ps --daemon_type=mds
```
section_path: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface > Procedure

title: Deploying the MDS service using the service specification
content:
Using the Ceph Orchestrator, you can deploy the MDS service using the service
specification.
section_path: Deploying the MDS service using the service specification

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor, and OSD daemons deployed.
section_path: Deploying the MDS service using the service specification > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Ensure that you have at least two pools, one for the Ceph File System (CephFS) data and one
for the CephFS metadata.
section_path: Deploying the MDS service using the service specification > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create the mds.yaml file.

```bash
touch mds.yaml
```
2. Edit the mds.yaml file.

```bash
service_type: mds
service_id: FILESYSTEM_NAME
placement:
 hosts:
 - HOST_NAME_1
 - HOST_NAME_2
 - HOST_NAME_3
```

For example,
```
service_type: mds
service_id: fs_name
placement:
 hosts:
 - host01
 - host02
```
3. Mount the YAML file under a directory in the container.For
example,
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell --mount mds.yaml:/var/lib/ceph/mds/mds.yaml
```
4. Navigate to the ceph/mds/ directory.For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# cd /var/lib/ceph/mds/
```
5. Log into the Cephadm shell.

```bash
cephadm shell
```
6. Navigate to the /ceph/mds/ directory.For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# cd /var/lib/ceph/mds/
```
7. Deploy MDS service using service specification.

```bash
ceph orch apply -i FILE_NAME.yaml
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 mds]# ceph orch apply -i mds.yaml
```
8. Once the MDS services is deployed and functional, create the CephFS.

```bash
ceph fs new CEPHFS_NAME METADATA_POOL DATA_POOL
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs new test metadata_pool data_pool
```
section_path: Deploying the MDS service using the service specification > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
Verify the MDS service deployment. 
1. List the service.
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls
```
2. List the hosts, daemons, and
processes.
```bash
ceph orch ps --daemon_type=DAEMON_NAME
```
For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ps --daemon_type=mds
```
section_path: Deploying the MDS service using the service specification > What to do next

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts added to the cluster.
- Root-level access to all the nodes.
- At least one MDS daemon deployed on the hosts.

title: About this task
content:
To remove the MDS service with the command-line interface, log in to the Cephadm
shell.
```bash
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
Use one of the following options to
remove MDS daemons.
section_path: Removing the MDS service using the Ceph Orchestrator > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Use the ceph orch rm command to remove the MDS service from the
entire cluster.
1. List the service.

```bash
ceph orch ls
```

For example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls
```
2. Remove the service.

```bash
ceph orch rm SERVICE_NAME
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch rm mds.test
```
section_path: Removing the MDS service using the Ceph Orchestrator > Procedure

title: Procedure
content:
1. Set the configuration parameter mon_allow_pool_delete to
`true`.

```bash
ceph config set mon mon_allow_pool_delete true
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph config set mon mon_allow_pool_delete true
```
2. Remove the file system, its data, and metadata pools.

```bash
ceph fs volume rm FILESYSTEM_NAME --yes-i-really-mean-it
```

This command also tries to remove the MDS using the enabled `ceph-mgr`
Orchestrator module.

```bash
ceph fs volume rm cephfs-new --yes-i-really-mean-it
```
For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs volume rm cephfs-new --yes-i-really-mean-it
```
section_path: Removing the MDS service using the Ceph Orchestrator > Procedure

title: Procedure
content:
List the hosts, daemons, and processes, by using the ceph orch ps
command.For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ps
```

title: Managing the NFS service gateway using the Ceph orchestrator
content:
As a storage administrator, you can use the Orchestrator with Cephadm in the backend to
deploy the NFS service gateway. Cephadm deploys NFS service using a predefined RADOS pool and
optional namespace.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 IBM supports CephFS exports only over the NFS v4.0+ protocol.

NFS service is an open source user-space NFS (Network File System) server that allows the export
of file systems with the NFS protocol.
section_path: Managing the NFS service gateway using the Ceph orchestrator

title: References
content:
For information on all the supported Ceph configurations, see:

- IBM Storage Ceph Supported configurations
section_path: Managing the NFS service gateway using the Ceph orchestrator > References

title: Prerequisites
content:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Root-level access to all the nodes.
- Hosts are added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor, and OSD daemons are deployed.
section_path: Managing the NFS service gateway using the Ceph orchestrator > Prerequisites

title: Creating the NFS service cluster
content: Create an NFS service cluster using the Ceph Orchestrator.
section_path: Creating the NFS service cluster

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts are added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor and OSD daemons are deployed.
section_path: Creating the NFS service cluster > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
You can create an NFS service cluster using the `mgr/nfs` module of the Ceph
Orchestrator. This module deploys the NFS cluster using Cephadm in the backend.

This creates a common recovery pool for all NFS service daemons, new user based on
`clusterid`, and a common NFS service config RADOS object.

For each daemon, a new user and a common configuration is created in the pool. Although all the
clusters have different namespaces with respect to the cluster names, they use the same recovery
pool.
section_path: Creating the NFS service cluster > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log into the Cephadm shell.For
example,
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. Enable the `mgr/nfs` module.

```bash
ceph mgr module enable nfs
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph mgr module enable nfs
```
3. Create the cluster.

```bash
ceph nfs cluster create CLUSTER_NAME ["HOST_NAME_1 HOST_NAME_2 HOST_NAME_3"]
```

The CLUSTER_NAME is an arbitrary string and HOST_NAME_1 is
an optional string signifying the hosts to deploy NFS service daemons.

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs cluster create nfsganesha "host01 host02"
NFS Cluster Created Successful
```
The NFS service cluster,
`nfsservice`, is created with one daemon on `host01` and
`host02`.
section_path: Creating the NFS service cluster > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
Verify the NFS service cluster.
- List the cluster details.
```bash
ceph nfs cluster ls
```
- Show NFS-Ganesha cluster
information.
```bash
ceph nfs cluster info CLUSTER_NAME
```
For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs cluster info nfsganesha
```
section_path: Creating the NFS service cluster > What to do next

title: Deploying the NFS service gateway using the command line interface
content:
You can use the Ceph Orchestrator with Cephadm in the backend to deploy the NFS service
gateway using the placement specification. In this case, you have to create a RADOS pool and create
a namespace before deploying the gateway.
section_path: Deploying the NFS service gateway using the command line interface

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts are added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor and OSD daemons are deployed.
section_path: Deploying the NFS service gateway using the command line interface > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 IBM supports CephFS exports only over the NFS v4.0+ protocol.
section_path: Deploying the NFS service gateway using the command line interface > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log into the Cephadm shell.For
example,
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. Create the RADOS pool namespace, and enable the application.For Ceph Block
Device (`rbd`) pools, enable
`rbd`.
```bash
ceph osd pool create POOL_NAME
ceph osd pool application enable POOL_NAME freeform/rgw/rbd/cephfs/nfs
rbd pool init -p POOL_NAME
```
For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool create nfs-pool
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool application enable nfs-pool nfs
[ceph: root@host01 /]# rbd pool init -p nfs-service
```
3. Deploy NFS service gateway using placement specification in the command line
interface.

```bash
ceph orch apply nfs SERVICE_ID --placement="NUMBER_OF_DAEMONS HOST_NAME_1 HOST_NAME_2 HOST_NAME_3"
```

The following example deploys an NFS service cluster `nfsservice`
with one daemon on `host01` and
`host02`.
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch apply nfs foo --placement="2 host01 host02"
```

title: What to do next
content:
- List the service.For example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls
```
- List the hosts, daemons, and
processes.

title: Deploying the NFS service gateway using the service specification
content:
You can use the Ceph Orchestrator with Cephadm in the backend to deploy the NFS service
gateway using the service specification. In this case, you have to create a RADOS pool and create a
namespace before deploying the gateway.
section_path: Deploying the NFS service gateway using the service specification

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts are added to the cluster.
section_path: Deploying the NFS service gateway using the service specification > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create the `nfs.yaml` file.For
example,
```
[root@host01 ~]# touch nfs.yaml
```
2. Edit the nfs.yaml specification file.

```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: SERVICE_ID
placement:
 hosts:
 - HOST_NAME_1
 - HOST_NAME_2
```

For example,
```
service_type: nfs
service_id: foo
placement:
 hosts:
 - host01
 - host02
```

- Optional: Enable the NLM to support locking for NFS protocol v3 support by adding
`enable_nlm: true` in the NFS.yaml specification
file.
```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: SERVICE_ID
placement:
 hosts:
 - HOST_NAME_1
 - HOST_NAME_2
spec:
 enable_nlm: true
```
For example,
```
service_type: nfs
service_id: foo
placement:
 hosts:
 - host01
 - host02
spec:
 enable_nlm: true
```
3. Mount the YAML file under a directory in the container.

```bash
cephadm shell --mount nfs.yaml:/var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml
```

For
example,
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell --mount nfs.yaml:/var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml
```
4. Create the RADOS pool, namespace, and enable RBD.

```bash
ceph osd pool create POOL_NAME
ceph osd pool application enable POOL_NAME rbd
rbd pool init -p POOL_NAME
```

For example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool create nfs-pool
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool application enable nfs-pool rbd
[ceph: root@host01 /]# rbd pool init -p nfs-pool
```
5. Navigate to the directory.For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# cd /var/lib/ceph/
```
6. Deploy NFS service gateway using service specification.

```bash
ceph orch apply -i FILE_NAME.yaml
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 ceph]# ceph orch apply -i nfs.yaml
```

content:

```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls
```
- List the hosts, daemons, and
processes.
```bash
ceph orch ps --daemon_type=DAEMON_NAME
```
For


title: Implementing HA for CephFS or NFS service
content:
You can deploy NFS with a high-availability (HA) front end, virtual IP by using the
`--ingress` flag and by specifying a virtual IP address. This deploys a combination
of `keepalived` and `HAProxy` and provides a high-availability NFS
front end for the NFS service.
section_path: Implementing HA for CephFS or NFS service

title: About this task
content:
When a cluster is created with `--ingress` flag, an ingress service is also
deployed to provide high-availability for the NFS servers. A virtual IP is used to provide a known,
stable NFS endpoint that all NFS clients can use to mount. Ceph handles the details of redirecting
NFS traffic on the virtual IP to the appropriate backend NFS servers and redeploys NFS servers when
they fail.

Deploying an ingress service for an existing service provides:
- A stable, virtual IP that can be used to access the NFS server.
- Failover between hosts when the hosts fail.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 When an `ingress` service is deployed on the NFS cluster, the
backend NFS service servers see the HAProxy’s IP address and not the client’s IP address. As a
result, if you are restricting client access based on IP address, access restrictions for NFS
exports will not work as expected.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 If the active NFS server serving a client goes down, the client’s I/Os are
interrupted until the replacement for the active NFS server is online and the NFS cluster is active
again.
section_path: Implementing HA for CephFS or NFS service > About this task

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts are added to the cluster.
- All the manager, monitor, and Tivoli Provisioning Manager for OS Deployment daemons are
deployed.
- Check that the NFS module is enabled.
section_path: Implementing HA for CephFS or NFS service > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log in to the Cephadm
shell.Example,
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. Create the NFS cluster with the `--ingress` flag.

```bash
ceph nfs cluster create CLUSTER_ID [PLACEMENT] [--port PORT_NUMBER] [--ingress --virtual-ip IP_ADDRESS/CIDR_PREFIX]
```

- Replace CLUSTER_ID with a unique string to name the NFS service cluster.
- Replace PLACEMENT with the number of NFS servers to deploy and the host or
hosts that you want to deploy the NFS Ganesha daemon containers on. The PLACEMENT
must be set to 1 to configure HAProxy.
- Use the `--port`
PORT_NUMBER flag to deploy NFS on a port other than the default port of
12049.
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 With ingress mode, the high-availability proxy takes port 2049 and NFS services are
deployed on 12049.
- The `--ingress` flag combined with the `--virtual-ip` flag,
deploys NFS with a high-availability front end (virtual IP).
- Replace `--virtual-ip`
IP_ADDRESS with an IP address to provide a known, stable NFS endpoint that all
clients can use to mount NFS exports. The `--virtual-ip` must include a CIDR prefix
length. The virtual IP is configured on the first identified network interface with an existing IP
in the same subnet.
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The number of hosts you allocate for the NFS service must be
greater than 1 to configure HAProxy. Specify the `placement: 1` parameter. In the
following example, HA is configured with one active NFS server and two hosts are
allocated.

Example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs cluster create mycephnfs "1 host02 host03" --ingress --virtual-ip 10.10.128.75/22
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Deployment of NFS daemons and the ingress service is asynchronous and the command
might return before the services have started.
3. Check that the services have started successfully.

```bash
ceph orch ls --service_name=nfs.CLUSTER_NAME
ceph orch ls --service_name=ingress.nfs.CLUSTER_NAME
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls --service_name=nfs.mycephnfs

NAME PORTS RUNNING REFRESHED AGE PLACEMENT
nfs.mycephnfs ?:12049 2/2 0s ago 20s host02;host03

[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls --service_name=ingress.nfs.mycephnfs

NAME PORTS RUNNING REFRESHED AGE PLACEMENT
ingress.nfs.mycephnfs 10.10.128.75:2049,9049 4/4 46s ago 73s count:2
```
section_path: Implementing HA for CephFS or NFS service > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
To verify that the services are properly implemented, perform one or both of the following:
- View the IP endpoints, IPs for the individual NFS daemons, and the virtual IP for the
`ingress`
service.
```bash
ceph nfs cluster info CLUSTER_NAME
```
Example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs cluster info mycephnfs

{
 "mycephnfs": {
 "virtual_ip": "10.10.128.75",
 "backend": [
 {
 "hostname": "host02",
 "ip": "10.10.128.69",
 "port": 12049
 },
 
 ],
 "port": 2049,
 "monitor_port": 9049
 }
}
```
- List the hosts and processes, by using the ceph orch ps | grep nfs
command.Example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ps | grep nfs
haproxy.nfs.nfsganesha.cali015.gvyawz host01 *:2049,9049 running (13h) 3m ago 13h 49.1M - 2.4.22-f8e3218 6c223bddea69 7c8e47dfd08f
keepalived.nfs.nfsganesha.cali015.tdrjuj host01 running (13h) 3m ago 13h 1559k - 2.2.8 09859a486cb9 62a88e6fe188
nfs.nfsganesha.0.0.cali015.zhxopd host01 *:12049 running (13h) 3m ago 13h 112M - 6.5 4d25f1e2e574 bc5c2aef63bd cef6e7959b0a ea02c0c50749
```

title: Deploying HA for CephFS or NFS using a specification file
content: Learn to deploy HA for Cepheus or NFS using a specification file.
section_path: Deploying HA for CephFS or NFS using a specification file

title: About this task
content:
You can deploy HA for Ceph or NFS using a specification file by first deploying an NFS service
and then deploying `ingress` to the same NFS service.
section_path: Deploying HA for CephFS or NFS using a specification file > About this task

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts are added to the cluster.
- All the manager, monitor, and OSD daemons are deployed.
- The NFS module is enabled.
section_path: Deploying HA for CephFS or NFS using a specification file > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log in to the Cephadm
shell.Example,
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. Ensure that the NFS module is
enabled.Example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph mgr module ls | more
```
3. Exit out of the Cephadm shell and create the nfs.yaml
file.Example,
```
[root@host01 ~]# touch nfs.yaml
```
4. Edit the nfs.yaml file to include the following details.Syntax,
```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: SERVICE_ID
placement:
 hosts:
 - HOST_NAME_1
 - HOST_NAME_2
 count: 1
spec:
 port: PORT_NUMBER
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 The number of hosts you allocate for the NFS service must be greater than 1
to configure HAProxy. Specify the `placement: 1` parameter.

Example,
```
service_type: nfs
service_id: cephfsnfs
placement:
 hosts:
 - host02
 - host03
 count: 1
spec:
 port: 12345
```
In this example, the server is run on the non default port of
`12345`, instead of the default port of `2049`, on host02 and
host03.
5. Mount the YAML file under a directory in the container.

```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell --mount nfs.yaml:/var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml
```
6. Log in to the Cephadm shell and navigate to the directory.

```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# cd /var/lib/ceph/
```
7. Deploy the NFS service by using service
specification.Syntax,
```bash
ceph orch apply -i FILE_NAME.yaml
```
Example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 ceph]# ceph orch apply -i nfs.yaml
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Deployment
of the NFS service is asynchronous and the command might return before the services have started
.
8. Check that the NFS services are started
successfully.Syntax,
```bash
ceph orch ls --service_name=nfs.CLUSTER_ID
```
Example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls --service_name=nfs.cephfsnfs

NAME PORTS RUNNING REFRESHED AGE PLACEMENT
nfs.cephfsnfs ?:12345 2/2 3m ago 13m host02;host03
```
9. Exit out of the Cephadm shell and create the ingress.yaml
file.Example,
```
[root@host01 ~]# touch ingress.yaml
```
10. Edit the `ingress.yaml` file to include the following
details.Syntax, 
```bash
service_type: SERVICE_TYPE
service_id: SERVICE_ID
placement:
 count: 1
spec:
 backend_service: SERVICE_ID_BACKEND
 frontend_port: FRONTEND_PORT
 monitor_port: MONITOR_PORT
 virtual_ip: VIRTUAL_IP_WITH_CIDR
```
Example,

```
service_type: ingress
service_id: nfs.cephfsnfs
placement:
 count: 1
spec:
 backend_service: nfs.cephfsnfs
 frontend_port: 2049
 monitor_port: 9000
 virtual_ip: 10.10.128.75/22
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 In this example, placement: count:
1 deploys the `HAProxy` service on random nodes. To specify the nodes to
deploy `HAProxy` on, use the `placement: hosts`
option:
```
service_type: ingress
service_id: nfs.cephfsnfs
placement:
 hosts:
 - host02
 - host03
```
11. Mount the YAML file under a directory in the container.Example,

```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell --mount ingress.yaml:/var/lib/ceph/ingress.yaml
```
12. Log in to the Cephadm shell and navigate to the directory.

```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# cd /var/lib/ceph/
```
13. Deploy the `ingress` service by using service
specification.Syntax,

```bash
ceph orch apply -i FILE_NAME.yaml
```
Example,

```
[ceph: root@host01 ceph]# ceph orch apply -i ingress.yaml
```
14. Check that the ingress services are started
successfully.Syntax,
```bash
ceph orch ls --service_name=ingress.nfs.CLUSTER_ID
```
Example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls --service_name=ingress.nfs.cephfsnfs

NAME PORTS RUNNING REFRESHED AGE PLACEMENT
ingress.nfs.cephfsnfs 10.10.128.75:2049,9000 4/4 4m ago 22m count:1
```

title: Updating the NFS service cluster
content:
You can update the NFS service cluster by changing the placement of the daemons on the
hosts with Cephadm in the backend.
section_path: Updating the NFS service cluster

title: Prerequisites
content:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts are added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor and OSD daemons are deployed.
- NFS service cluster created using the `mgr/nfs` module.
section_path: Updating the NFS service cluster > Prerequisites

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log into the Cephadm shell:

Example

```bash
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. Update the cluster:

Syntax

```bash
ceph orch apply nfs CLUSTER_NAME ["HOST_NAME_1,HOST_NAME_2,HOST_NAME_3"]
```

The *CLUSTER_NAME* is an arbitrary string, *HOST_NAME_1* is an optional string
signifying the hosts to update the deployed NFS service daemons.

Example

```bash
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch apply nfs nfsservice "host02"
```

This updates the `nfsservice` cluster on `host02`.
section_path: Updating the NFS service cluster > Procedure

title: Verification
content:
- List the cluster details:

Example

```bash
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs cluster ls
```
- Show NFS-Ganesha cluster information:

Syntax

```bash
ceph nfs cluster info CLUSTER_NAME
```

Example

```bash
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs cluster info nfsservice
```
- List the hosts, daemons, and processes:

Syntax

```bash
ceph orch ps --daemon_type=DAEMON_NAME
```

Example

```bash
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ps --daemon_type=nfs
```

title: Prerequisites

section_path: Removing the NFS service  gateway > Prerequisites

title: Procedure

title: NFS specific Kerberos setup
content:
You need to create service principals for both NFS server and client. The respective keys
are stored in the keytab files. These principals are required to set up the initial security context
required by GSS_RPCSEC.
section_path: NFS specific Kerberos setup

title: About this task
content:
The service principals have format like `nfs/@REALM`. You can copy the
*/etc/krb5.conf* file from the working system to the Ceph nodes.
section_path: NFS specific Kerberos setup > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create service principal for that host:

```bash
[root@host ~]# kinit admin/admin

Password for admin/admin@PUNE.IBM.COM: 
[root@host ~]# kadmin
Authenticating as principal admin/admin@PUNE.IBM.COM with password.
Password for admin/admin@PUNE.IBM.COM:
kadmin: addprinc -randkey nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com
No policy specified for nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM; defaulting to no policy
Principal "nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM" created.
```
2. Add the key to the keytab file:

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 During this step, you are already on the NFS server and using `kadmin`
interface. Here, the keytab operations reflect on the keytab of the NFS server.

```bash
kadmin: ktadd nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com

Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes256-cts-hmac-sha384-192 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type camellia256-cts-cmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type camellia128-cts-cmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type arcfour-hmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
kadmin:
```
3. Run step 1 and 2 on all the Ceph nodes where NFS service containers are running and all
the NFS clients.

title: NFS service container settings
content: Learn how to configure the NFS service settings in the Ceph environment.
section_path: NFS service container settings

title: Procedure
content:
1. Retrieve the existing NFS service container configuration:

```bash
[ceph: root@host /]# ceph orch ls --service-type nfs --export

service_type: nfs
service_id: c_service
service_name: nfs.c_service
placement:
 hosts:
 - host1
 - host2
 - host3
spec:
 port: 2049
```
2. Modify the container configuration to pass on /etc/krb5.conf and
/etc/krb5.keytab files to the container from the host. These files will be
referred by NFS service at runtime to validate incoming service tickets and secure the communication
between NFS service and NFS client (`krb5p`).

```bash
[root@host ~]# cat nfs.yaml

service_type: nfs
service_id: c_service
service_name: nfs.c_service
placement:
 hosts:
 - host1
 - host2
 - host3
spec:
 port: 2049
extra_container_args:
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.keytab:/etc/krb5.keytab:ro"
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.conf:/etc/krb5.conf:ro"
```
3. Make the modified nfs.yaml file available inside the cephadm
shell:

```bash
[root@host ~]# cephadm shell --mount nfs.yaml:/var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml

Inferring fsid ff1c1498-73ec-11ee-af38-fa163e9a17fd
Inferring config /var/lib/ceph/ff1c1498-73ec-11ee-af38-fa163e9a17fd/mon.ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer/config
Using ceph image with id 'fada497f9c5f' and tag 'ceph-8.0-rhel-9-containers-candidate-73711-20231018030025' created on 2024-10-18 03:03:39 +0000 UTC
registry-proxy.engineering.ibm.com/rh-osbs/rhceph@sha256:e66e5dd79d021f3204a183f5dbe4537d0c0e4b466df3b2cc4d50cc79c0f34d75
```
4. Verification: Validate whether the file has the required changes:

```bash
[ceph: root@host /]# cat /var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml

service_type: nfs
service_id: c_service
service_name: nfs.c_service
placement:
 hosts:
 - host1
 - host2
 - host3
spec:
 port: 2049
extra_container_args:
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.keytab:/etc/krb5.keytab:ro"
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.conf:/etc/krb5.conf:ro"
```
5. Apply the required changes to NFS service container and redeploy the container:

```bash
[ceph: root@host /]# ceph orch apply -i /var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml

Scheduled nfs.c_service update...
[ceph: root@ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer /]# ceph orch redeploy nfs.c_ganesha
Scheduled to redeploy nfs.c_service.1.0.ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer.sxzuts on host 'ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer'
Scheduled to redeploy nfs.service.2.0.ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node2.psuvki on host 'ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node2'
Scheduled to redeploy nfs.c_service.0.0.ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node3.qizzvk on host 'ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node3'
```
6. Verification: Validate whether the redeployed service has the required changes:

```bash
[ceph: root@host /]# ceph orch ls --service-type nfs --export

service_type: nfs
service_id: c_service
service_name: nfs.c_service
placement:
 hosts:
 - ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer
 - ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node2
 - ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node3
extra_container_args:
- -v
- /etc/krb5.keytab:/etc/krb5.keytab:ro
- -v
- /etc/krb5.conf:/etc/krb5.conf:ro
spec:
 port: 2049
```
7. Modify the export definition to have `krb5*` (`krb5`,
`krb5i`, `krb5p`) security flavor:

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You can create such an export after completing the above setup.

```bash
[ceph: root@host /]# ceph nfs export info c_service/exp1

{
 "access_type": "RW",
 "clients": [],
 "cluster_id": "c_service",
 "export_id": 1,
 "fsal": {
 "fs_name": "fs1",
 "name": "CEPH",
 "user_id": "nfs.c_ganesha.1"
 },
 "path": "/volumes/_nogroup/exp1/81f9a67e-ddf1-4b5a-9fe0-d87effc7ca16",
 "protocols": [
 4
 ],
 "pseudo": "/exp1",
 "sectype": [
 "krb5"
 ],
 "security_label": true,
 "squash": "none",
 "transports": [
 "TCP"
 ]
}
```

maximum file and size quotas and to create and delete snapshots for the specific directory.
Subvolumes

content:
As a storage administrator, you can manage the NFS exports that use Ceph Object Gateway
or CephFS as the backstore on the Ceph Dashboard. You can deploy and configure, edit and delete the
NFS service daemons directly from the dashboard.

The dashboard manages NFS service configuration files that are stored in RADOS objects on the
Ceph Cluster. NFS service must store part of their configuration in the Ceph cluster.

title: Rate-limiting in NFS
content:
Learn about the rate-limiting or quality of service (QoS) in NFS.

With the rate-limiting or QoS (quality of service) feature in NFS you can control the client’s
read/write bandwidth and rate-limiting of the client's input/output operations (IOPS). This function
operates at export and client levels, controlling read/write requests and IOPS. QoS ensures that all
clients accessing backend storage receives a fair share of resources.

You can enable QoS for a single node NFS server and multiple instances of NFS servers.

The QoS configuration must be stored in the RADOS object and be accessible by any NFS server
within the server group. Also, each export must reside on only one NFS server within the group.

The QoS function in NFS supports both bandwidth control and IOPS control.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The rate-limiting feature is supported only for NFS version 4 and later.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS

title: Bandwidth rate-limiting
content:
NFS bandwidth rate limiting allows administrators to control the amount of bandwidth that NFS
clients use when accessing or transferring data from an NFS server. This helps prevent excessive
network congestion, ensures fair bandwidth distribution, and optimizes network performance for all
users and applications.

The following are supported options in bandwidth rate-limiting:

Per share (export) bandwidth control
Use this option to configure the maximum bandwidth that is allowed per share
(export). In this case, QoS makes sure that the cumulative bandwidth of all clients
accessing this export does not exceed the set bandwidth. For example, if the bandwidth limit for an
export is set to 100 Mbps, any client performing any operation on this export is given only 100 Mbps
speed.
Per client bandwidth control
Use this option to configure the maximum bandwidth that is allowed per client. In this case,
even if the client accesses more than one export, the total bandwidth that is given to the client
will not exceed the set limit. For example, if the client bandwidth is set to 100 Mbps, this client
can perform operations on any exports with only 100 Mbps speed.
PerShare-perClient bandwidth control
Use this option to configure both per share maximum bandwidth and per client maximum bandwidth.
In this case, the maximum client bandwidth is controlled to the set limit, while the maximum per
export bandwidth is also maintained. 
For example, if the per export bandwidth is set to 200 Mbps
and the bandwidth per client is set to 100 Mbps, client A writing to this export will have a speed
of 100 Mbps. If client B writes to the same export, client B will have a rate limit of 100 Mbps, as
100 Mbps is already in use by client A.

In bandwidth rate-limiting, you can configure the maximum read and write bandwidth individually.
For example, you can set the maximum write bandwidth to 100 Mbps and the read bandwidth to 200
Mbps.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS > Bandwidth rate-limiting

title: Input/output operations (IOPS) rate-limiting
content:
IOPS rate-limiting is a feature that controls the number of input/output operations per second
that NFS clients can perform on an NFS server. This helps prevent performance degradation, ensures
fair resource allocation, and optimizes storage system efficiency.

Read and write operations consist of multiple underlying tasks. For example, a write operation
includes four tasks: get file, open file, write file, and put file. If you set the IOPS limit to 20,
only 5 IOPS allowed for each of these tasks.

The following are supported options in IOPS rate-limiting are:

Per export operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum number of IOPS allowed per export. In this case, QoS
makes sure that the cumulative number of operations that are performed by all clients accessing this
export will not exceed the given limit. For example, if the IOPS limit is set to 20, then any client
accessing this export can perform only 5 IOPS.
Per client operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum number of operations that are allowed per client.
Irrespective of the number of exports that the client is accessing, the total number of operations
that are performed by the client will not exceed this limit. For example, if the IOPS limit for a
client is set to 20, then this client can perform only 5 IOPS, irrespective of the number of exports
it is accessing.
Per export-per client operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum that is allowed per export and maximum that is allowed
per client operations. The total number of operations that are performed by the client is controlled
to the set limit. Simultaneously, QoS helps ensure the maximum operations per export limit is kept
within the limits. For example, if the IOPS limit for export is set to 20 and the client limit is
set to 40, then this client can perform only 5 operations on the export as its limit is set to 20.
The client can perform the remaining 3 operations on other exports.

For IOPS rate-limiting, all operations that the client performs are counted together as a single
unit.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS > Input/output operations (IOPS) rate-limiting

content:

title: About this task
content:
Rate-limiting is also known as quality of service (QoS). Defining bandwidth limits
helps ensure a balanced workload distribution across the cluster.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The bandwidth rate limiting for NFS clusters ranges from a minimum of 1 MiB to a maximum of
100 GiB.

For more information, see Rate-limiting in NFS.

title: Setting bandwidth rate-limiting
content:
Learn to set the bandwidth rate-limiting for an NFS cluster by using the
dashboard.

title: Before you begin
content:

- An NFS cluster.
section_path: Managing bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS cluster > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
1. From the Dashboard navigation, go to File > NFS.
2. Select the NFS cluster for which you want to set the QoS and click Set
QOS.The Create NFS cluster form displays.
3. Complete the form, per your requirements.
1. Client ID is prepopulated with the selected cluster
name.

title: Managing SMB service, shares, and clusters
content:
Learn about the SMB file system, how to manage the SMB service, shares and clusters by
using the IBM Storage Ceph dashboard.

Samba is an open source implementation of the Server message Block (SMB) protocol that provides
file and print services between clients across various operating systems.

The Ceph MGR module for SMB provides an interface for deploying and controlling clusters of Samba
services and managing SMB shares. In the `SMB manager` module, a cluster is a logical
management unit that maps to one or more managed Samba services that itself is a cluster and might
or might not use any high-availability mechanisms.

The orchestration is automatically triggered when a cluster is configured for at least one share.
The placement field of the cluster resource is passed on to the orchestration layer and is used to
determine on what nodes of the Ceph cluster SMB containers can run.

Currently, SMB services can listen on port 445 only. Due to this restriction, only one Samba
server, as part of one cluster, can run on a single Ceph node at a time. Ensure that the placement
specs on each cluster do not overlap.

The SMB clusters are fully isolated from each other. If you have sufficient resources in your
Ceph cluster, you can run multiple independent clusters that can or cannot join the same Active
Directory (AD) domains or forests. You cannot share a directory with multiple different clusters
that can have different authentication modes or identity-mapping schemes.
section_path: Managing SMB service, shares, and clusters

Standalone
This mode allows you to manually define and manage user accounts and groups within Ceph. It is

cluster with Standlone as the authentication mode, see Creating users and groups access resources.
Active Directory (AD) 
This mode integrates with an existing Active Directory domain, enabling centralized

integration with enterprise environments. To create an SMB cluster with AD as
the authentication mode, see Creating Active Directory access resources.

title: SMB overview dashboard
content:
Learn about the SMB overview dashboard.

The SMB overview dashboard provides a real-time visualization of SMB (Server Message Block)
protocol activity and performance across your Ceph cluster. SMB is commonly used for file sharing in
networked environments, and this dashboard enables you to monitor key performance indicators such as
throughput, latency, session activity, and I/O operations.

This dashboard is intended for use by system administrators, performance engineers, and support
personnel responsible for maintaining high availability and performance of SMB services

Ensure that the monitoring stack is installed. For more information, see Deploying the monitoring stack.

Go to the Ceph dashboard > File > SMB > Overview to view the dashboard. You can also access the dashboard from
Ceph
dashboard > Administration > Services > Grafana > SMB
Overview.

To use the dashboard effectively,

- Use the time range selector in the upper-right to adjust the visibility window for metrics.
- Use filters such as Ceph cluster, Hostname and
SMB service to go into specific nodes or clusters.
- Look for latency and I/O spikes, which can indicate performance degradation or high usage
periods.
- Refer to this dashboard during troubleshooting, capacity planning, and performance tuning.

Dashboard pages and descriptions:
SMB metrics status
The operational status of the Prometheus exporter collecting SMB metrics. A green “Up” status
means that the exporter is running and metrics are actively used.

SMB active sessions
The number of currently active SMB sessions in the cluster.

SMB shares activity
The current activity across all SMB shares within the cluster.

SMB ingress throughput
The rate at which data is received by the SMB server, which is measured in bytes (B). Helps
monitor incoming data load from clients.

SMB latency
The average latency for SMB operations, which are measured in microseconds (µs). Useful for
identifying performance issues; lower latency values indicate better responsiveness.

SMB egress throughput
The rate at which data is sent out from the SMB server, which is measured in bytes (B).

SMB I/O
The number of SMB input/output operations per second across all nodes. Shows a quick view of
overall I/O activity.

SMB throughput (Graph)
A time series graph plotting ingress and egress throughput across the monitored period. Helps
identify usage patterns, peaks, and anomalies over time.

SMB latencies (Graph)
A time series visualization of SMB operation latencies (for example, create, close, flush) for
each node.
section_path: SMB overview dashboard

title: Managing CephFS snapshots
content:
As a storage administrator, you can cretate Ceph File System (CephFS) volume and
subvolume snapshots on the IBM Storage Ceph dashboard.

The Ceph File System (CephFS) snapshots create an immutable, point-in-time view of a Ceph File
System. CephFS snapshots are asynchronous and are kept in a special hidden directory in the CephFS
directory named .snap. You can specify snapshot creation for any directory
within a Ceph File System. When specifying a directory, the snapshot also includes all the
subdirectories beneath it.

CephFS snapshot feature is enabled by default on new Ceph File Systems, but it must be manually
enabled on existing Ceph File Systems.

**Warning:** **Note:** Warning:
 Each Ceph Metadata Server (MDS) cluster allocates the snap identifiers
independently. Using snapshots for multiple Ceph File Systems that are sharing a single pool causes
snapshot collisions, and results in missing file data.
section_path: Managing CephFS snapshots

title: Scheduling CephFS snapshots
content:
As a storage administrator, you can schedule Ceph File System (CephFS) snapshots on the
IBM Storage Ceph dashboard.

Scheduling Ceph File System (CephFS) snapshots ensures consistent reliable backups at regular
intervals, reducing the risk of data loss. Scheduling snapshots also provides ease of management by
reducing administrative overhead of manually managing backups.

A list of available snapshots for a particular file system, subvolume, or directory is found on
the File > File Systems page.
Use the snapshot list for creating scheduled backups.
section_path: Scheduling CephFS snapshots

title: Creating CephFS snapshot schedule
content:

on the IBM Storage Ceph dashboard.

title: Before you begin
content: - A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
section_path: Creating CephFS snapshot schedule > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Create a policy for automatic creation of Ceph File System (CephFS) snapshot of a volume or a
certain directory. You can also define how often you want to schedule it (for example: every hour,
every day, every week, etc.)

You can specify the number of snapshots or a period for which you want to keep the snapshots. All
the older snapshots are deleted when the number of snapshots exceeds or when the retention period is
over
section_path: Creating CephFS snapshot schedule > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. From the dashboard navigation, go to
File > File
Systems.File system volumes are listed. Select the file system
where you want to create the snapshot schedule.
2. Go to Snapshot schedules tab.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The Enable is available only if the *snapshot_scheduler *is
disabled on the cluster.

1. **Optional: **Click Enable to enable the
`snapshot_scheduler` module.After enabling the scheduler, wait for the
dashboard to reload and navigate back to the Snapshot schedule
page.
2. Click Create.The Create Snapshot
schedule form opens.
3. Enter the directory name, start date, start time, and schedule.

- Directory: You can search by typing in the path of the directory or
subvolume and select the directory from the suggested list where you want to create the snapshot
schedule.
- Start date: Enter date on which you want the scheduler to start creating
the snapshots. By default the current date is selected.
- Start time: Enter the time at which you want the scheduler to start
creating the snapshots. By default the current time is added.
- Schedule: Enter the number of snapshots and the frequency at which you
want to create the snapshots. Frequency can be hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly or lastest
snapshots.

1. **Optional: **Click Add retention policy if you want to
add retention policy to the schedule. You can add multiple retention policies. Enter the
number of snapshots and the frequency at which you want to retain the snapshots. Frequency can be
hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly or lastest snapshots.
2. Click Create snapshot schedule.A notification is
displayed that the snapshot schedule is created successfully.
section_path: Creating CephFS snapshot schedule > Procedure

title: Deploying NFS service with Ceph Object Storage backend
content:
Using the Ceph Orchestrator, you can deploy the NFS service in Ceph Object
Gateway.
section_path: Deploying NFS service with Ceph Object Storage backend

title: Before you begin
content:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Root-level access to all the nodes.
- Hosts are added to the cluster.
- All Manager, Monitor, RGW, and OSD daemons are deployed.
section_path: Deploying NFS service with Ceph Object Storage backend > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log into the Cephadm shell.

```bash
cephadm shell
```
2. Create a NFS specification file with the relevant data, including
the host on which the NFS service needs to be installed.

```bash
cat nfs-conf.yml

service_type: nfs
service_id: nfs-rgw-service
placement:
 hosts: ['host1']
spec:
 port: 2049
```
3. Apply the NFS service via the specification file created in step 2.

```bash
ceph orch apply -i nfs-conf.yml
```
4. Verify if the NFS service has been created successfully.

```bash
ceph orch ls --service_name nfs.nfs-rgw-service --service_type nfs
```
section_path: Deploying NFS service with Ceph Object Storage backend > Procedure

title: Exporting the namespace to NFS service
content:
Configure and manage NFS service exports for use with the Ceph Object
Gateway.
section_path: Exporting the namespace to NFS service

title: Before you begin
content:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- A user created. For more information, see Create a user.
section_path: Exporting the namespace to NFS service > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
You can manage the NFS service exports that use Ceph Object Gateway as the backend via the IBM Storage Ceph dashboard. See Managing NFS service exports for more information.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- IBM supports only NFS version 4 exports using the Ceph Object Gateway.

You can only create user-level NFS service exports by using the command-line-interface (CLI).
section_path: Exporting the namespace to NFS service > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log in to the Cephadm shell.

Syntax

```bash
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. Create the user-level export in the root directory.

Syntax

```bash
ceph nfs export create rgw --cluster-id NFS_CLUSTER_NAME --pseudo-path PATH_FROM_ROOT --user-id USER_ID
```

Example

```
[ceph:root@host01 /]# ceph nfs export create rgw --cluster-id cluster1 --pseudo-path root/testnfs1/ --user-id nfsuser
```
3. Mount the NFS.

Syntax

```bash
mount -t nfs IP_ADDRESS:PATH_FROM_ROOT -osync MOUNT_POINT
```

Example

```
[ceph:root@host01 /]# mount -t nfs 10.0.209.0:/root/testnfs1 -osync /mnt/mount1
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 For large uploads >200 GB, mounting with `-osync` might affect
the input/output operations. Use S3 with multi-part to upload such objects.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 If you run `setattr` on the buckets, it silently prevents setting attributes on
paths representing buckets.
section_path: Exporting the namespace to NFS service > Procedure

title: Ceph File Systems
content:
As a storage administrator, you can configure the Ceph Metadata Server (MDS) and how to create, mount, and work the Ceph File System (CephFS). Get to know the features, system components, and limitations to manage a CephFS environment.

The Ceph File System (CephFS) is a file system compatible with POSIX standards that is built on top of the Ceph distributed object store, RADOS (Reliable Autonomic Distributed Object Storage). CephFS provides file access to an IBM Storage Ceph cluster, and uses the POSIX semantics wherever possible. For example, in contrast to many other common network file systems like NFS, CephFS maintains strong cache coherency across clients. The goal is for processes that use the file system to behave the same when they are on different hosts as when they are on the same host. However, sometimes CephFS diverges from the strict POSIX semantics.

The Ceph File System has the following features:
 
Parallel Data Streams
CephFS is a parallel filesystem. Clients and storage servers can exchange data through multiple-streams in parallel, which helps increase throughput and scalability.
Scalability
The Ceph File System is highly scalable due to horizontal scaling of metadata servers and direct client reads and writes with individual OSD nodes.
Shared file system
The Ceph File System is a shared file system so multiple clients can work on the same file system simultaneously.
Multiple file systems
You can have multiple file systems active on one storage cluster. Each CephFS has its own set of pools and its own set of Metadata Server (MDS) ranks. When deploying multiple file systems this requires more running MDS daemons. This can increase metadata throughput, but also increases operational costs. You can also limit client access to certain file systems.
High availability
The Ceph File System provides a cluster of Ceph Metadata Servers (MDS). One is active and others are in standby mode. If the active MDS stops unexpectedly, one of the standby MDS becomes active. As a result, client mounts continue working through a server failure. This behavior makes the Ceph File System highly available. In addition, you can configure multiple active metadata servers.
Configurable file and directory layouts
The Ceph File System allows users to configure file and directory layouts to use multiple pools, pool namespaces, and file striping modes across objects.
POSIX Access Control Lists (ACL)
The Ceph File System supports the POSIX Access Control Lists (ACL). ACLs are enabled by default with the Ceph File Systems mounted as kernel clients with kernel version `kernel-3.10.0-327.18.2.el7` or newer. To use an ACL with the Ceph File Systems mounted as FUSE clients, you must enable them.
Client Quotas
The Ceph File System supports setting quotas on any directory in a system. The quota can restrict the number of bytes or the number of files that are stored beneath that point in the directory hierarchy. CephFS client quotas are enabled by default.

- For more information about installing Ceph Metadata servers, see Managing the MDS service.
- For more information about creating Ceph File Systems, see Deploying the CephFS.

title: Using CephFS
content:
Understand how Ceph File Systems (CephFS) integrates within the Ceph cluster, its data
flow, the role of the Metadata Server (MDS) and aspects of volume management.
section_path: Using CephFS

title: Understanding the CephFS data flow
content:
Understand the data flow in CephFS to
recognize the interactions between the CephFS client, Metadata Server (MDS), and the Ceph Storage
Cluster.

Figure 1 illustrates the role of Metadata Server in CephFS.

Figure 1. CephFS Data Flow
The
following are the primary functions of the CephFS Client and Metadata Server:
CephFS Client

Mounting
Connects to CephFS by using either `kcephfs` or `ceph-fuse`.
Metadata requests
Requests metadata from the MDS for file operations.

Metadata Server

Metadata Operations
Manages file system metadata including file creation, directory management, and access control.

Caching
Improves performance by caching frequently accessed metadata. Caching is distributed and
coordinated with clients and other multi-MDS

Ceph Storage Cluster

RADOS Storage
Handles distributed object storage.
OSDs
Manage data storage, retrieval, and replication across the cluster. 

Data Access and Storage

Accessing Data
After retrieving metadata from the MDS, the client accesses data directly from OSDs. Data is
stored as objects within the Ceph Storage Cluster, with the CRUSH algorithm ensuring efficient
distribution and redundancy.

title: Comparison with other FSaaS Solutions
content:
Following are some of the key comparisons between CephFS and other SaaS solutions:
Scalability
CephFS inherits all the benefits of the core Ceph internal storage engine RADOS. File systems
can be increased in capacity and performance by adding more storage nodes. The data is automatically
distributed and protetected.
Performance
CephFS is a parallel filesystem. Datastreams can run in parallel from multiple CephFS clients to
multiple Ceph storage servers and OSDs. Metadata operations are running independently of the data
operations.
Integration
CephFS is a POSIX-compatible file system. The integration of applications and infrastructure
software such as Backup and Recovery solutions can rely on the POSIX nature of CephFS.
Feature Set
CephFS provides parallel data access and throughput and performance can be scaled up and down by
the number of storage nodes and storage devices. CephFS like the rest of Ceph is designed to have no
single point of failure and data redundancy is a built-in feature of the Ceph RADOS architecture.
Available physical storage capacities are managed in thinly provisioned pools which all share the
same infrastructure. CephF subvolumes can also be exported through NFS or SMB to clients that help
enable many more use-cases.
section_path: Using CephFS > Comparison with other FSaaS Solutions

title: Data Protection in CephFS
content:
Because CephFS builds on top of RADOS, it inherits all the data durability available from that
system. File data and metadata are regularly scrubbed and node failures are automatically handled.
CephFS also provides metadata scrubbing that you can start.

For geographically resilient scale storage, you can use CephFS snapshots and your favorite file
system backup solution to generate consistent versions. If a data center disaster occurs, CephFS
provides fsck like tools to rebuild the file system from data objects. For help if your system
reports data issues, contact IBM Support.
section_path: Using CephFS > Data Protection in CephFS

title: Health messages
content:
Understand the different health messages for the Ceph File System.

For more information, see Configuring Metadata Server daemons.
section_path: Health messages

title: Cluster health checks
content:
The Ceph Monitor daemons generate the following health messages in response to certain states of
the Metadata Server (MDS):

mds rank(s) <ranks> have failed

One or more MDS ranks are not currently assigned to any MDS daemon. The storage cluster will not
recover until a suitable replacement daemon starts.

mds rank(s) <ranks> are damaged

One or more MDS ranks has encountered severe damage to its stored metadata, and cannot start
again until the metadata is repaired.

mds cluster is degraded

One or more MDS ranks are not currently up and running, clients might pause metadata I/O until
this situation is resolved. This includes ranks being failed or damaged, and includes ranks which
are running on an MDS but are not in the `active` state yet — for example, ranks in
the `replay` state.

mds <names> are laggy

The MDS daemons are supposed to send beacon messages to the monitor in an interval specified by
the `mds_beacon_interval` option, the default is 4 seconds. If an MDS daemon fails to
send a message within the time specified by the `mds_beacon_grace` option, the
default is 15 seconds. The Ceph Monitor marks the MDS daemon as `laggy` and
automatically replaces it with a standby daemon if any is available.
section_path: Health messages > Cluster health checks

title: Daemon-reported health checks
content:
The MDS daemons can identify a variety of unwanted conditions, and return them in the output of
the `ceph status` command. These conditions have human readable messages, and also
have a unique code starting `MDS_HEALTH`, which appears in JSON output.

Behind on trimming…

**Code:** MDS_HEALTH_TRIM

CephFS maintains a metadata journal that is divided into log segments. The length of journal (in
number of segments) is controlled by the `mds_log_max_segments` setting. When the
number of segments exceeds that setting, the MDS starts writing back metadata so that it can remove
(trim) the oldest segments. If this process is too slow, or a software bug is preventing trimming,
then this health message appears. The threshold for this message to appear is for the number of
segments to be double `mds_log_max_segments`.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Increasing `mds_log_max_segments` is recommended if the trim warning is
encountered. However, ensure that this configuration is reset back to its default when the cluster
health recovers and the trim warning is seen no more. It is recommended to set
`mds_log_max_segments` to 256 to allow the MDS to catch up with trimming.

Client NAME failing to respond to capability release

**Code:**
MDS_HEALTH_CLIENT_LATE_RELEASE, MDS_HEALTH_CLIENT_LATE_RELEASE_MANY

CephFS clients are issued capabilities by the MDS. The capabilities work like locks. Sometimes,
for example, when another client needs access, the MDS requests clients to release their
capabilities. If the client is unresponsive, it might fail to do so promptly, or fail to do so at
all. This message appears if a client has taken a longer time to comply than the time specified by
the `mds_revoke_cap_timeout` option (default is 60 seconds).

Client NAME failing to respond to cache pressure

**Code:**
MDS_HEALTH_CLIENT_RECALL, MDS_HEALTH_CLIENT_RECALL_MANY

Clients maintain a metadata cache. Items, such as inodes, in the client cache, are also pinned in
the MDS cache. When the MDS needs to shrink its cache to stay within its own cache size limits, the
MDS sends messages to clients to shrink their caches too. If a client is unresponsive, it can
prevent the MDS from properly staying within its cache size, and the MDS might eventually run out of
memory and terminate unexpectedly. This message appears if a client has taken more time to comply
than the time specified by the `mds_recall_state_timeout` option (default is 60
seconds). For more information, see Metadata Server cache size limits.

Client NAME failing to advance its oldest client/flush tid

**Code:**
MDS_HEALTH_CLIENT_OLDEST_TID, MDS_HEALTH_CLIENT_OLDEST_TID_MANY

The CephFS protocol for communicating between clients and MDS servers uses a field called
oldest tid to inform the MDS of which client requests are fully complete so
that the MDS can forget about them. If an unresponsive client is failing to advance this field, the
MDS might be prevented from properly cleaning up resources used by client requests. This message
appears if a client has more requests than the number specified by the
`max_completed_requests` option (default is 100000) that are complete on the MDS side
but have not yet been accounted for in the client’s `oldest tid` value.

Metadata damage detected

**Code:**
MDS_HEALTH_DAMAGE

Corrupt or missing metadata was encountered when reading from the metadata pool. This message
indicates that the damage was sufficiently isolated for the MDS to continue operating, although
client accesses to the damaged subtree return I/O errors. Use the `damage ls`
administration socket command to view details on the damage. This message appears as soon as any
damage is encountered.

MDS in read-only mode

**Code:**
MDS_HEALTH_READ_ONLY

The MDS has entered into read-only mode and will return the EROFS
error codes to client operations that attempt to modify any metadata. The MDS enters into read-only
mode:
section_path: Health messages > Daemon-reported health checks (part 1)

title: Daemon-reported health checks
content:
- If it encounters a write error while writing to the metadata pool.
- If the administrator forces the MDS to enter into read-only mode by using the
force_readonly administration socket command.

N slow requests are blocked

**Code:**
MDS_HEALTH_SLOW_REQUEST

One or more client requests have not been completed promptly, indicating that the MDS is either
running very slowly, or encountering a bug. Use the `ops` administration socket
command to list outstanding metadata operations. This message appears if any client requests have
taken more time than the value specified by the `mds_op_complaint_time` option
(default is 30 seconds).

Too many inodes in cache

**Code:**
MDS_HEALTH_CACHE_OVERSIZED

The MDS has failed to trim its cache to comply with the limit set by the administrator. If the
MDS cache becomes too large, the daemon might exhaust available memory and terminate unexpectedly.
By default, this message appears if the MDS cache size is 50% greater than its limit.
