title: Windows 11 desktop client side mount options for NFSv3 fileshare
content:
Use this information to understand the client side mount options for NFSv3
fileshare.

NFSv3 (version 3) is supported and enabled for clients that do not yet support NFSv4.2 mounts for
CephFS file shares.
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Mount a file share with NFSv3 Windows 11 desktop only when NFSv4.2 is not
supported on the client or server side. For more information about configuring NFS, see Configuring
NFS Service daemons.

Use the following mount client-side options to mount a file share with NFSv3 Windows 11
desktop:

```bash
Usage: mount [-o options] [-u:username] [-p:<password | *>] <\\computername\sharename> <devicename | *>
```

| Mount options | Description |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| -o rsize=size | Set the size of the read buffer in kilobytes. |
| -o wsize=size | Set the size of the write buffer in kilobytes. |
| -o timeout=time | Set the timeout value in seconds for an RPC call. |
| -o retry=number | Set the number of retries for a soft mount. |
| -o mtype=soft|hard | Set the mount type. |
| -o lang=euc-jp|euc-tw|euc-kr|shift-jis|big5|ksc5601|gb2312-80|ansi | Specify the encoding used for file and directory names. |
| -o fileaccess=mode | Specify the permission mode of the file. These are used for new files created on NFS servers. Specified using UNIX style mode bits. |
| -o nolock | Disable locking. |
| -o anon | Mount as an anonymous user. |
| -o casesensitive=yes|no | Specify case sensitivity of file lookup on server. |
| -o sec=sys|krb5|krb5i|krb5p | Specify the security mechanism for mounting an NFS share. This value can include any of the following: sec=sys: No authentication or security checks are performed. Data transfers are not encrypted. sec=krb5: Specifies Kerberos authentication for mounting the NFS share. sec=krb5i: Extends Kerberos security by adding data integrity checks between the client and server hasn't been tampered. sec=krb5p: Enhances Kerberos security by enabling data privacy, which encrypts data exchanged between the client and server. |
section_path: Windows 11 desktop client side mount options for NFSv3 fileshare

title: Rate-limiting in NFS
content:
With the rate-limiting or QoS (quality of service) feature in NFS you can control the
client’s read/write bandwidth and rate-limiting of the client's input/output operations (IOPS). This
function operates at export and client levels, controlling read/write requests and IOPS. QoS helps
ensures that all clients accessing backend storage receives a fair share of resources.

You can enable QoS for a single node NFS server and multiple instances of NFS servers.

The QoS configuration must be stored in the RADOS object and be accessible by any NFS server
within the server group. Also, each export must reside on only one NFS server within the group.

The QoS function in NFS supports both bandwidth control and IOPS control.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The rate-limiting feature is supported only for NFS version 4 and later.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS

title: Bandwidth rate-limiting
content:
NFS bandwidth rate limiting allows administrators to control the amount of bandwidth that NFS
clients use when accessing or transferring data from an NFS server. This helps prevent excessive
network congestion, ensures fair bandwidth distribution, and optimizes network performance for all
users and applications.

The following are supported options in bandwidth rate-limiting:

Per share (export) bandwidth control
Use this option to configure the maximum bandwidth that is allowed per share
(export). In this case, QoS makes sure that the cumulative bandwidth of all clients
accessing this export does not exceed the set bandwidth. For example, if the bandwidth limit for an
export is set to 100 Mbps, any client running any operation on this export is given only 100 Mbps
speed.
Per client bandwidth control
Use this option to configure the maximum bandwidth that is allowed per client. In this case,
even if the client accesses more than one export, the total bandwidth that is given to the client
will not exceed the set limit. For example, if the client bandwidth is set to 100 Mbps, this client
can perform operations on any exports with only 100 Mbps speed.
Per share (export)-per client bandwidth control
Use this option to configure both per share maximum bandwidth and per client maximum bandwidth.
In this case, the maximum client bandwidth is controlled to the set limit, while the maximum per
export bandwidth is also maintained. 
For example, if the per export bandwidth is set to 200 Mbps
and the bandwidth per client is set to 100 Mbps, client A writing to this export will have a speed
of 100 Mbps. If client B writes to the same export, client B will have a rate limit of 100 Mbps, as
100 Mbps is already in use by client A.

In bandwidth rate-limiting, you can configure the maximum read and write bandwidth individually.
For example, you can set the maximum write bandwidth to 100 Mbps and the read bandwidth to 200
Mbps.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS > Bandwidth rate-limiting

title: Input/output operations (IOPS) rate-limiting
content:
IOPS rate-limiting is a feature that controls the number of input/output operations per second
that NFS clients can run on an NFS server. This helps prevent performance degradation, ensures fair
resource allocation, and optimizes storage system efficiency.

Read and write operations consist of multiple underlying tasks. For example, a write operation
includes four tasks: get file, open file, write file, and put file. If you set the IOPS limit to 20,
only 5 IOPS allowed for each of these tasks.

The following are supported options in IOPS rate-limiting are:

Per export operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum number of IOPS allowed per export. In this case, QoS
makes sure that the cumulative number of operations that are performed by all clients accessing this
export will not exceed the given limit. For example, if the IOPS limit is set to 20, then any client
accessing this export can run only 5 IOPS.
Per client operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum number of operations that are allowed per client.
Regardless of the number of exports that the client is accessing, the total number of operations
that are performed by the client will not exceed this limit. For example, if the IOPS limit for a
client is set to 20, then this client can perform only 5 IOPS, irrespective of the number of exports
it is accessing.
Per export-per client operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum that is allowed per export and maximum that is allowed
per client operations. The total number of operations that are run by the client is controlled to
the set limit. Simultaneously, QoS helps ensure the maximum operations per export limit is kept
within the limits. For example, if the IOPS limit for export is set to 20 and the client limit is
set to 40, then this client can run only 5 operations on the export as its limit is set to 20. The
client can run the remaining 3 operations on other exports.

For IOPS rate-limiting, all operations that the client runs are counted together as a single
unit.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS > Input/output operations (IOPS) rate-limiting

title: Managing rate-limiting for NFS clusters
content:
Learn to manage the rate-limiting or quality of service (QoS) for NFS clusters.

There are 2 types of rate-limiting for NFS clusters:
- Bandwidth rate-limiting.
- Input/output (IOPS) rate-limiting.

You can enable and disable the rate-limiting feature by using the command line.
section_path: Managing rate-limiting for NFS clusters

title: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS cluster
content:
Learn to enable the bandwidth rate-limiting feature by using the command
line.
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS cluster

title: About this task
content:
You can define bandwidth limits per client or share (per export) to ensure a balanced workload
distribution across the cluster.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The bandwidth rate-limiting, the limit ranges from a minimum of 1 Mbps to a maximum of 4
Gbps.
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS cluster > About this task

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A healthy and running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- An NFS cluster.
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS cluster > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
Run the following command to enable bandwidth rate-limiting for an NFS
cluster.
```bash
ceph nfs cluster qos enable bandwidth_control CLUSTER ID qos_type:PerShare|PerClient|PerShare_PerClient [--combined-rw-bw-ctrl] [--max_export_write_bw VALUE] [--max_export_read_bw VALUE] [--max_client_write_bw VALUE] [--max_client_read_bw VALUE] [--max_export_combined_bw VALUE] [--max_client_combined_bw VALUE]
```
 Where, 
- CLUSTER_ID is the NFS cluster ID.
- qos_type is the type of bandwidth control. You can select either
PerShare (per export), PerClient or
PerShare_PerClient based on your requirement.
- If the PerShare qos_type is selected, the cluster-level quality of service
(QoS) configuration applies to all exports created on that NFS cluster. If
combined-rw-bw-ctrl is set to false, you must specify both the
max_export_write_bw and max_export_read_bw parameters.
Otherwise, only the max_export_combined_bw parameter is required.
- If the PerClient qos_type is selected, the cluster-level QoS configuration
applies to all clients accessing exports on that cluster. If
combined-rw-bw-ctrl is set to false, you must specify both the
max_client_write_bw and max_client_read_bw parameters.
Otherwise, only the max_client_combined_bw parameter is required
- If the PerShare_PerClient qos_type is selected, the cluster-level
configuration applies to all exports and all clients of that NFS cluster. If
combined-rw-bw-ctrl is set to false, you must specify the
max_export_write_bw, max_export_read_bw,
max_client_write_bw, and max_client_read_bw parameters.
Otherwise, only the max_export_combined_bw and
max_client_combined_bw parameters are required.
- combined-rw-bw-ctrl This parameter enables combined read and write
bandwidth. If combined-rw-bw-ctrl is set to true, then only 
max_export_combined_bw and max_client_combined_bw parameters are
allowed based on QoS type.
- max_export_write_bw is the maximum bandwidth for export write per
second.
- max_export_read_bw is the maximum bandwidth for export that is read per
second.
- max_client_write_bw is the maximum bandwidth that the client can use for
writing per second.
- max_client_read_bw is the maximum bandwidth that the client can use for
reading per second.
- max_export_combined_bw is the maximum combined read/write bandwidth for
export per second.
- max_client_combined_bw is the maximum combined read/write bandwidth for
client per second.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You can specify the value as 10, 10 MB, 10 MiB, or 10 GB.

Example of bandwidth rate-limiting for PerShare,
clust_nfs is the NFS cluster ID

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos enable bandwidth_control clust_nfs PerShare --max_export_write_bw 100MB --max_export_read_bw 200MB
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos get clust_nfs
{
 "combined_rw_bw_control": false,
 "enable_bw_control": true,
 "enable_iops_control": false,
 "enable_qos": true,
 "max_export_read_bw": "200.0MB",
 "max_export_write_bw": "100.0MB",
 "qos_type": "PerShare"
}
```

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos get clust_nfs
{
```

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos get clust_nfs
```

content:

title: Procedure
content:
Run the following command to enable bandwidth rate-limiting for an NFS cluster.

```bash
$ ceph nfs cluster qos enable ops_control CLUSTER_ID qos_type:PerShare|PerClient|PerShare_PerClient [max_export_iops VALUE] [max_client_iops VALUE]
```

Where, 
- CLUSTER_ID is the NFS cluster ID.
- <qos_type> is the type of ops control. It can be
PerShare, PerClient or
PerShare_PerClient.
- - If PerShare qos_type is selected, then the cluster-level QoS configuration
applies to all exports created on that NFS cluster. It requires the
<export_ops_count> parameter.
- If PerClient qos_type is selected, then the cluster-level QoS configuration
applies to all clients accessing exports created on that cluster. It requires the
<client_ops_count> parameter.
- If PerShare_PerClient qos_type is selected, then the cluster-level
configuration applies to all exports as well as all clients of that NFS cluster. It requires both
<export_ops_count> and <client_ops_count>
parameters.
- <max_export_iops> is the count of IOPS operations for an export.
- <max_client_iops> is the count of IOPS operations for a client of an
export.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 If this command is used to update the qos_type, make sure to update
all the exports with the required parameters.

Example of IOPS rate-limiting for PerShare_PerClient,
clust_nfs is the NFS cluster ID

```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs cluster qos enable ops_control clust_nfs PerShare_PerClient --max_export_iops 2000 --max_client_iops 3000

{
 "combined_rw_bw_control": true,
 "enable_bw_control": true,
 "enable_iops_control": true,
 "enable_qos": true,
 "max_client_combined_bw": "200.0MB",
 "max_client_iops": 3000,
 "max_export_combined_bw": "200.0MB",
 "max_export_iops": 2000,
 "qos_type": "PerShare_PerClient"
}
```

title: Managing rate-limiting for NFS exports
content:
Learn to manage the rate-limiting or quality of service (QoS) for NFS exports.

There are 2 types of rate-limiting for NFS exports:
- Bandwidth rate-limiting.
- Input/output (IOPS) rate-limiting.

You can enable and disable the rate-limiting feature by using the command line.
section_path: Managing rate-limiting for NFS exports

title: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS export
content:
Learn how to enable bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS exports by using the command
line.
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS export

title: About this task
content:
Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS exports helps control network traffic by restricting
data transfer rate for NFS clients. Bandwidth rate-limiting prevents network congestion, ensures
fair bandwidth distribution, and optimizes system performance.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You cannot enable export-level bandwidth control if the cluster-level
qos_type is PerClient.
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS export > About this task

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A healthy and running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- An NFS cluster.
- NFS exports.
section_path: Enabling bandwidth rate-limiting for NFS export > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
The following command enables and updates QoS bandwidth control for export.

To enable export-level bandwidth control, you must enable cluster-level bandwidth control with
qos_type
PerShare or Pershare_PerClient. This command creates
QOS_BLOCK in the export block.

```bash
$ nfs export qos enable bandwidth_control CLUSTER_ID <pseudo_path> [--combined-rw-bw-ctrl] [--max_export_write_bw VALUE] [--max_export_read_bw VALUE] [--max_client_write_bw VALUE] [--max_client_read_bw VALUE] [--max_export_combined_bw VALUE] [--max_client_combined_bw VALUE]
```
 Where,
- CLUSTER_ID is the NFS cluster ID.
- pseudo_path is the pseudo-root path. (The path must be an absolute
path.)
- combined-rw-bw-ctrl enables combined read and write bandwidth control. When
set to True, only the max_export_combined_bw and 
max_client_combined_bw parameters are allowed, depending on the qos_type.
- max_export_write_bw is the maximum bandwidth that can be used for export
write per second.
- max_export_read_bw is the maximum bandwidth that can be used for export
that is read per second.
- max_client_write_bw is the maximum bandwidth that the client can use for
writing per second.
- max_client_read_bw is the maximum bandwidth that the client can use for
reading per second.
- max_export_combined_bw is the maximum combined read/write bandwidth for
export per second.
- max_client_combined_bw is the maximum combined read/write bandwidth for
client per second.
Example for bandwidth rate-limiting for QoS type
Pershare_PerClient
```
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs export qos enable bandwidth_control clust_nfs /export1 --max_export_write_bw 100MB --max_export_read_bw 200MB --max_client_write_bw 300MB --max_client_read_bw 100MB
[ceph: root@ceph-node-0 /]# ceph nfs export qos get clust_nfs /export1
{
 "cluster_enable_bw_control": true,
 "cluster_enable_iops_control": false,
 "cluster_enable_qos": true,
 "combined_rw_bw_control": false,
 "enable_bw_control": true,
 "enable_qos": true,
 "max_client_read_bw": "100.0MB",
 "max_client_write_bw": "300.0MB",
 "max_export_read_bw": "200.0MB",
 "max_export_write_bw": "100.0MB"
}
```

title: Procedure
content:
You can disable bandwidth rate-limiting for the NFS exports by using the following
command:
```bash

```

Where, 
- CLUSTER_ID is the NFS cluster ID.
- PSEUDO_PATH is the pseudo-root path. (The path must be an absolute
path.)
This command disables QoS bandwidth control for exports, allowing them to use
unlimited input/output bandwidth. Once export QoS is disabled, the exports will no longer follow the
bandwidth values set at the cluster level.
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 To use cluster level QoS bandwidth control values
for export again, you can use the NFS export apply CLUSTER_ID command, with the
export section not having QOS_BLOCK.

title: Kerberos encryption with Ceph NFS services
content:
Learn how Kerberos encryption works with Ceph NFS services.

Ceph NFS services supports secure authentication and data integrity through Kerberos, a network
authentication protocol that uses symmetric encryption and trusted third-party verification. When
Kerberos is enabled, Ceph NFS services clients and the server authenticate each other using tickets
that are issued by the Key Distribution Centre (KDC), eliminating the need for password-based
authentication over the network.

Kerberos integration with Ceph NFS services is typically configured through GSS-API (Generic
Security Services API), which allows RPCSEC_GSS (Remote Procedure Call Security by using GSS) to
handle the authentication and encryption layers. This setup supports various levels of security,
including:

- `AUTH_SYS`: Standard UNIX authentication (nonencrypted, used for
compatibility).
- `AUTH_GSS/KRB5`: Kerberos-based authentication.
- `krb5i`: Kerberos with integrity protection.
- `krb5p`: Kerberos with both integrity and privacy (encryption).

When clients mount an NFS share by using Kerberos (for example, sec=krb5, krb5i, or krb5p), all
communication is secured according to the specified level. Encryption helps ensure secure access
control and data-in-transit protection, making Ceph NFS services a viable choice for enterprise
environments requiring strong authentication and encrypted communication.
section_path: Kerberos encryption with Ceph NFS services

title: Enabling encryption by using Kerberos for Ceph NFS services
content:
Learn to configure Kerberos encryption with Ceph NFS services by using the command-line
interface.

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running and IBM Storage Ceph 8.1 cluster.
- Ceph NFS services are installed and configured on the server.
- A working Kerberos Key Distribution Centre (KDC).
- Ensure that the domain name is present for all the nodes in the Ceph cluster and NFS client
nodes. Use the Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN).
- The NFS Ganesha node is time synchronised with KDC
section_path: Enabling encryption by using Kerberos for Ceph NFS services > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Use this procedure to configure the Ceph File System (CephFS) to work with Ceph NFS services
using Kerberos-based security. This setup provides strong authentication and protects client/server
communication over the network.

Kerberos support in Ceph NFS services is available from version 4.0 onward. Ensure that your Ceph
cluster is running a supported version of Ceph NFS services.
section_path: Enabling encryption by using Kerberos for Ceph NFS services > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Set up the Kerberos client.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The Kerberos client machine must be time-synchronised with the KDC. It is advised to sync KDC
and clients by using NTP. A time difference of 5 minutes or more leads to Kerberos authentication
failure and throws a clock skew error.

1. Check whether you have the following RPMs. If not, install them using the dnf
install command.

```
[root@ceph-host ~]# rpm -qa | grep krb5
krb5-libs-1.20.1-9.el9_2.x86_64
```

title: Disabling Kerberos encryption for Ceph NFS services
content:
Learn to disable Kerberos encryption on an NFS cluster using the command
line.
section_path: Disabling Kerberos encryption for Ceph NFS services

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- Running and healthy IBM Caph Storage 8.1 cluster.
- Ceph NFS services is installed and configured on the server.
- Kerberos encryption enabled.
section_path: Disabling Kerberos encryption for Ceph NFS services > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
To disable Kerberos encryption for the Ceph NFS services, you can configure
the cluster to either

- Not use Kerberos at all (falling back to `sec=sys`)
- Use Kerberos authentication (krb5) but disable privacy encryption by not using krb5p.

In both scenarios, changes to the NFS export definition are required. A system administrator
must implement these changes, which involve modifying server-side configuration files typically
/etc/exports.
An alternative approach is to adjust the mount options on the
client side This method is only applicable if the existing export definition on the server already
includes the sys option under the sectype parameter.
section_path: Disabling Kerberos encryption for Ceph NFS services > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Unmount the
export.Syntax
```bash
umount EXPORT_NAME
```

```
$ umount mnt/nfs
```
2. Modify the configuration file (ganesha.config) to remove encryption. In the
`Export` section, change `SecType=sys` to disable Kerberos
encryption.

```
SecType=”sys”
```
3. Mount the export again with the updated configuration file.

```bash
mount -t nfs GANESHA_HOST_NAME:PSEUDO_PATHMOUNT_POINT
```

```
$ mount -t nfs 192.168.10.10:/foo /mnt
```
section_path: Disabling Kerberos encryption for Ceph NFS services > Procedure

title: SMB clusters and share management
content:
Samba is an open source implementation of the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol that
provides file and print services between clients across various operating systems.

Samba uses the SMB
protocol to share files and printers across a network connection. Operating systems that support
this protocol include Microsoft Windows, Mac OS (X), and Linux.

The Ceph MGR module for SMB provides an interface for deploying and controlling clusters of Samba
services and managing SMB shares. In the `SMB manager` module, a cluster is a logical
management unit that maps to one or more managed Samba services that itself is a cluster and may or
may not use any high-availability mechanisms.
section_path: SMB clusters and share management

title: Enabling the SMB services
content:
Before communicating with the Ceph MGR module for SMB, it must be enabled first.

```bash
ceph mgr module enable smb
```

Usually, SMB is layered on CephFS subvolumes or subvolume groups. Do not create any SMB shares on
top of CephFS root volumes. You can share a subvolume once or more within a single SMB cluster
context. However, defining only one SMB share per CephFS subvolume is recommended to keep complexity
low.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 NFS and SMB file services cannot share the same subvolume as mixed protocol support for NFS
and SMB is not supported currently and doing so can potentially cause data corruption.

Ceph managed SMB services only support the SMB2 and SMB3 versions of the protocol. The SMB1
version of the protocol, also known as CIFS, is not supported. Systems such as the Linux kernel,
provide tools for both SMB1 and SMB2+ under the CIFS moniker. Check the documentation of the
software packages used to help ensure that they support SMB2+ regardless of how the tool is
named.
section_path: SMB clusters and share management > Enabling the SMB services

title: Managing SMB clusters and shares
content:
The Ceph MGR SMB module automatically deploys logical clusters on hosts by
using cephadm orchestration.

This orchestration is automatically triggered when a cluster is configured for at least one
share. The placement field of the cluster resource is passed on to the orchestration layer and is
used to determine on what nodes of the Ceph cluster SMB containers can run.

Currently, SMB services can listen on port 445 only. Due to this restriction, only one Samba
server, as part of one cluster, may run on a single Ceph node at a time. Ensure that the placement
specs on each cluster do not overlap.

The SMB clusters are fully isolated from each other. If there are sufficient resources in your
Ceph cluster, you can run multiple independent clusters that can or cannot join the same Active
Directory (AD) domains or forests. You cannot share a directory with multiple different clusters
that can have different authentication modes or identity mapping schemes.

You can interact with the Ceph MGR SMB module by using the following methods.

Imperative method
This method uses the ceph smb commands to interact with the Ceph MGR SMB
module. 
For more information, see Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method.

Declarative method
This method uses the `resources specification file` either in YAML or JSON
format.
For more information, see Composing resource specifications for declarative method.
section_path: Managing SMB clusters and shares

title: Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method
content: Learn how to create, list, or remove SMB clusters by using imperative specific command-line instructions.
section_path: Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- Ensure that the SMB module is configured with `cephadm` orchestration to function properly.
- Gather information about the domain if you are using active-directory.
- Create a domain user to join to active directory (AD).
- Determine whether you need to use custom_dns setting.
- Which users to define if you are not using AD.
- Set the earmark for SMB. For more information see, Earmarking a file system subvolume.
section_path: Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method > Before you begin

title: About this task
content: This method uses commands like ceph smb cluster create and ceph smb cluster rm, similar to those used in Ceph NFS manager module on the command line.
section_path: Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method > About this task

title: Creating SMB clusters
content:
Create SMB clusters by using the imperative method.

Create a new logical cluster, which is identified by the cluster ID value. The cluster create command must specify the authentication mode the cluster uses. Authentication mode is either custom users or groups, also known as a stand-alone server, with the `user` keyword.
 
```bash
ceph smb cluster create CLUSTER_ID {user} [--domain-realm=DOMAIN_REALM] 
[--domain-join-user-pass=DOMAIN_JOIN_USER_PASS] 
[--define-user-pass=DEFINE_USER_PASS] [--custom-dns=CUSTOM_DNS] 
[--placement=PLACEMENT] [--clustering=CLUSTERING]
```

For example,
 
```
auth_mode: user
[ceph: root@host01 ~]# ceph smb cluster create smb1 user --define_user_pass user1%passwd --placement label:smb --clustering default

auth_mode: AD
[ceph: root@host01 ~]# ceph smb cluster create smb1 active-directory --domain_realm samba.qe --domain_join_user_pass Administrator%RT@123 --custom_dns 10.71.34.153 --placement label:smb --clustering default
```

Table 1 lists the parameters that are required for creating the cluster.
 
| Parameters | Description |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| auth_mode | Specify either user or active-directory. |
| cluster_id | A unique string identifying the cluster. |
| clustering | Optional. Control if a cluster abstraction actually uses SMB’s clustering mechanism. The value may be one of default, always, or never. A default value indicates that clustering should be enabled if the placement count value is any value other than 1. A value of always enables clustering regardless of the placement count. A value of never disables clustering regardless of the placement count. If unspecified, default is assumed. |
| custom_dns | IP addresses to override default DNS resolvers. |
| define_user_pass | Authentication details for a user in the user-auth mode in the form <username>%<password>. This parameter accepts multiple username and password combinations. For example, --define-user-pass=alice%foo --define-user-pass=bob%bar --define-user-pass=charlie%baz |
| domain_join_user_pass | Credentials in the form <username>%<password> for joining SMB servers to the AD domain. |
| domain_realm | Required for Active Directory setups. |
| password_filter | Optional. One of none or base64. If the filter is none the password values on the command line are assumed to be plain text. If the filter is base64 the password values are assumed to be obscured with base64 encoding the string. If --password-filter-out is not specified this filter will also be applied to the output. |
| password_filter_out | Optional. One of none, base64, or hidden. If the filter is none the password fields in the output are emitted as plain text. If the filter is base64 password fields will be obscured by base64 encoding the string. If the filter is hidden the password values will be replaced by an invalid generic replacement string containing only asterisks. |
| placement | A specification for Ceph orchestration placement. |
| public_addrs | Optional. A string in the form of <ipaddress/prefixlength>[%<destination interface>]. Supported only when using SMB’s clustering. Assign virtual IP addresses that will be managed by the clustering subsystem and may automatically move between nodes running SMB containers. |
section_path: Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method > Creating SMB clusters

title: Listing SMB clusters
content:
By listing SMB clusters, you can help ensure robust data protection and efficient management. The listing of cluster IDs output defaults to JSON. Select YAML encoding with the --format=yaml option.
 List all SMB clusters by using the smb cluster ls command.
 
```bash
ceph smb cluster ls [--format=FORMAT]
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 ~]# ceph smb cluster ls
[
 "smb1"
]
```
section_path: Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method > Listing SMB clusters

title: Removing SMB clusters
content:
Delete an SMB cluster by using the imperative method.
 
```bash
ceph smb cluster rm CLUSTER_ID
```

section_path: Managing SMB shares by using imperative method > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Create a new SMB share, hosted by the named cluster, that maps to the given CephFS volume
and path.

```bash
ceph smb share create CLUSTER_ID SHARE_ID CEPHFS_VOLUME PATH [--share-name=SHARE_NAME] [--subvolume=SUBVOLUME_NAME] [--readonly]
```

Use the CLUSTER_ID that is provided while creating the SMB cluster. For more
information, see Managing SMB clusters by using imperative method.

Table 1 lists the parameters that are required for creating the
cluster.
| Parameters | Description |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| cluster_id | A short string uniquely identifying the cluster. |
| share_id | A short string uniquely identifying the share |
| cephfs_volume | The name of the CephFS volume to be shared. |
| path | A path relative to the root of the volume and/or subvolume. |
| share_name | Optional. The public name of the share, visible to clients. If not provided the share_id will be used automatically. |
| subvolume | Optional. A subvolume name in the form [<subvolumegroup>/]<subvolume>. The option causes the path to be relative to the CephFS subvolume specified. |
| readonly | Creates a read-only share. |

title: Procedure
content:
You can view all the resources that are applied to the Ceph cluster configuration by
using the ceph smb show command.

```bash
ceph smb show [RESOURCE_NAME...]
```

This example shows one cluster resource (if it exists) for the cluster
cluster1 along with all the shared resources that are associated with the
cluster1.
```
$ ceph smb show ceph.smb.cluster.bob ceph.smb.share.Cluster1
```
The
show command shows all resources of a given type or specific resources by ID.
resource_name arguments can take the following forms:
| Resource name | Description |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| ceph.smb.cluster | Shows all cluster resources. |
| ceph.smb.cluster.cluster_id | Shows the cluster with given cluster ID. |
| ceph.smb.share | Shows all shared resources. |
| ceph.smb.share.cluster_id | Shows all shared resources part of the specific cluster. |
| ceph.smb.share.cluster_id.share_id | Shows specific shared resources with the specific cluster and share IDs. |
| ceph.smb.usersgroups | Shows all Users & Groups resources. |
| ceph.smb.usersgroups.users_goups_id | Shows specific Users & Groups resource. |
| ceph.smb.join.auth | Shows all join auth resources. |
| ceph.smb.join.auth.auth_id | Shows a specific join auth resource. |

title: SMB File System share access right and control management
content:
Learn about SMB share access rights and access control.

Clients can connect to the servers after a cluster and its component containers are deployed and
the shares are configured. Microsoft Windows systems have SMB support that is built in and using
Windows Explorer a share can be specified as:

`\\<hostname>\<sharename>.`

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 IP addresses must be added in the DNS to use the host names.
For example,
`\\ceph0.mycluster.sink.test\Staff Pics`. The Windows node automatically attempts to
log in to the share. If the cluster and Windows client are configured for the same AD Domain, a
password-less single sign-on login is automatically performed. A username and password prompt
appears if the cluster is configured for user authentication. Enter one username and password
combination that was specified in the cluster or the `ceph.smb.usersgroups`
resource.

MacOS X systems and many Linux based systems also support connecting to SMB shares.
section_path: SMB File System share access right and control management

title: Encryption support in SMB
content:
SMB supports end-to-end encryption to protect data in transit between clients and
servers, helping ensure secure data transmission and access control.

When integrating Ceph with SMB, encryption support is enabled on the server at the protocol level
for SMB 3.x versions, which include AES-based encryption algorithms. Encryption helps guarantees
that all SMB traffic, including file transfers, remains secure even when traversing untrusted
networks.

Encryption in SMB is enabled by default and when the SMB client establishes a connection with an
SMB server, it negotiates encryption capabilities during the SMB session setup. If encryption is
required, all subsequent messages are automatically encrypted before transmission.

| SMB protocol version | Encryption algorithm |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| SMB 3.0 | AES-128-CCM |
| SMB 3.0.2 | AES-128-CCM |
| SMB 3.1.1 | AES-128-CCM, AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, AES-256-CCM |

**Important:** **Note:** Important:

- Setting per share encryption is not supported.
- Enabling and disabling specific algorithms for SMB version 3.1.1 is not supported.
section_path: Encryption support in SMB

title: SMB Multichannel (Technology Preview)
content:
The SMB Multichannel feature enables file servers to use multiple network connections simultaneously.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Technology Preview features are not supported with IBM production service level agreements (SLAs), might not be functionally complete, and IBM does not recommend using them for production. These features provide early access to upcoming product features, enabling customers to test functionality and provide feedback during the development process.

The SMB Multichannel feature facilitates aggregation of network bandwidth and fault tolerance when multiple paths are available between the SMB 3.x client and the SMB 3.x server. This capability allows server applications to take full advantage of all available network bandwidth and makes them resilient to network failures.

SMB Multichannel channel provides the following capabilities:

Higher throughput

The file server can simultaneously transmit more data by using multiple connections for high-speed or multiple network adapters.

Network fault tolerance

When clients simultaneously use multiple network connections, the clients can continue without interruption despite losing a network connection.

Automatic configuration:

SMB Multichannel automatically discovers multiple available network paths and dynamically adds connections as necessary.

In SMB Multichannel feature, the client negotiates SMB3 protocol and multichannel capability with the SMB server. The client then looks for available interfaces, and the SMB server provides the interface list, such as Receive Side Scaling (RSS) and network speed through the SMB File System Control (FSCTL) operation. The SMB client transparently chooses an appropriate setup and uses multiple channels based on the client workload, Network Interface Card (NIC) number, speed, and properties.
section_path: SMB Multichannel (Technology Preview)

title: Understanding SMB Multichannel requirements
content:
Requirements for using the SMB Multichannel feature are as follows:

- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster with multiple SMB servers
- SMB shares
- SMB clients supporting SMB3
- At least one of the following configurations:
 
- Multiple network adapters
- One or more network adapters that support RSS
- One or more network adapters that are configured by using NIC Teaming

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 SMB Multichannel is not supported on servers where clustering is disabled. SMB server instances that are not part of a cluster cannot retrieve network interface information from the operating system, which is required for SMB Multichannel functionality.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 SMBDirect is not supported and is out of scope for multichannel.
section_path: SMB Multichannel (Technology Preview) > Understanding SMB Multichannel requirements

title: Configuring SMB Multichannel
content: SMB Multichannel is enabled by default and automatically detects and uses multiple network connections when the configuration is identified.
section_path: SMB Multichannel (Technology Preview) > Configuring SMB Multichannel

title: Configuring name normalization in CephFS
content:
Learn how to set directory entry name normalization and
the `ceph.dir.charmap` virtual attribute in CephFS.
section_path: Configuring name normalization in CephFS

title: How normalization works
content:
CephFS uses Unicode normalization to ensure consistent handling of directory names. It supports
the following Unicode normalization forms:
nfd:
Canonical decomposition (default)
nfc
Canonical decomposition followed by canonical composition
nfkd
Compatibility decomposition
nfkc
Compatibility decomposition followed by canonical composition

When a client performs a path traversal or lookup, it applies the configured normalization form
to each directory entry name before sending the request to the Ceph Metadata Server (MDS). The MDS
stores only the normalized names and uses them for comparisons and lookups.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 If you set the normalization value to an empty string, the MDS restores the default,
`nfd`.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The MDS maintains an `alternate_name` metadata (also used for encryption) for
directory entries which allows the client to persist the original un-normalized name used by the
application. The MDS does not interpret this metadata in any way; it’s only used by clients to
reconstruct the original name of the directory entry.
section_path: Configuring name normalization in CephFS > How normalization works

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- CephFS must be configured and running.
- Target directory must be empty and not part of a snapshot.
- You must have appropriate authorization to modify extended attributes on the directory.
section_path: Configuring name normalization in CephFS > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
1. Run the setfattr command to configure the desired normalization form
for a directory.

```bash
setfattr -n ceph.dir.normalization -v <normalization> <directory>/
```

For example,
```
setfattr -n ceph.dir.normalization -v nfc foo/ 

getfattr -n ceph.dir.normalization foo/ 

# file: foo/ 

ceph.dir.normalization="nfc"
```
2. Verify the normalized setting.

```bash
getfattr -n ceph.dir.normalization foo/
```

For example,
```
ceph.dir.normalization="nfc"
```
section_path: Configuring name normalization in CephFS > Procedure

title: Configuring case folding in CephFS
content:
Learn how to configure case sensitivity for directory entry names in CephFS using the
`ceph.dir.casesensitive` and `ceph.dir.charmap` virtual attributes. By
default, CephFS treats directory names as case-sensitive, following POSIX behavior. You can disable
case sensitivity (enable case folding) to allow case-insensitive comparisons for a directory and its
sub-directories.
section_path: Configuring case folding in CephFS

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- Directory must be empty.
- Directory must not be part of a snapshot.
- The client has `p` (path) MDS capabilities to modify virtual extended attributes.
This applies to all `ceph.dir.charmap` attributes, including normalization.
section_path: Configuring case folding in CephFS > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
1. Set the directory to be case-insensitive.

```bash
setfattr -n ceph.dir.casesensitive -v <bool <directory>
```

For example,
```
setfattr -n ceph.dir.casesensitive -v 0 foo/
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Setting case sensitivity automatically enables the default normalization form
`nfd`.
2. Verify the case sensitivity setting.

```bash
getfattr -n ceph.dir.casesensitive foo/ 

# file: foo/ 

ceph.dir.casesensitive="0"
```

For example,
```
# file: foo/
ceph.dir.casesensitive="0"
```
3. Verify the updated character map.

```bash
getfattr -n ceph.dir.charmap <directory>/
```

```bash
getfattr -n ceph.dir.charmap foo/ 

# file: foo/ 

ceph.dir.charmap="{\"casesensitive\":false,\"normalization\":\"nfd\",\"encoding\":\"utf8\"}"
```
section_path: Configuring case folding in CephFS > Procedure

title: Troubleshooting SMB in a Ceph environment
content:
Learn how to troubleshoot common SMB issues in a Ceph environment.

This section provides essential troubleshooting guidance for diagnosing and resolving issues that
are related to SMB (Server Message Block) services in a Ceph environment. It focuses on three key
areas:

Testing client connectivity
Learn how to verify connectivity between the Windows client and Ceph SMB services by using basic
network and share access checks.
Measuring SMB throughput
Understand how to measure data transfer performance between the SMB share and the Windows client
to identify any bottlenecks or inconsistencies.
Validating VIPs and failover
Test the functions of Virtual IPs (VIPs) and ensure proper failover behavior if there is node or
service disruptions to maintain high availability.

These troubleshooting steps can help isolate issues, validate configurations, and ensure that the
SMB integration in your Ceph cluster operates reliably and efficiently.
section_path: Troubleshooting SMB in a Ceph environment

title: Measuring SMB throughput by using Robocopy
content:
Learn to measure SMB throughput between the SMB share and the Windows client by using the
in-built robocopy utility in Windows.
section_path: Measuring SMB throughput by using Robocopy

title: About this task
content:
To assess the data transfer performance between the SMB share and the Windows client, use the
built-in robocopy utility. This helps identify potential performance bottlenecks or latency issues
in the SMB communication.
section_path: Measuring SMB throughput by using Robocopy > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. On the Windows client, open a command prompt with administrative privileges.
2. Run the following command to copy a large test file or directory from the local system to
the mounted SMB share (or vice versa):

```bash
robocopy C:\path\to\source \\<smb-server>\sharename /E /Z /NP /R:0 /W:0 /LOG:robocopy_log.txt
```

Where, 
C:\path\to\source
Is the path of the test data.

\\<smb-server>\sharename
Is the SMB share path.

/Z switch
The /Z switch enables restartable mode, /NP disables progress display for better performance,
and /LOG logs the output.
3. After completion, check the robocopy_log.txt file for the following
metrics:

- Bytes transferred
Transfer time

Throughput (in MB/min)

These metrics can help determine whether throughput is within expected limits based on your
network and storage setup. If performance is lesser than expected, investigate factors such as
network latency, SMB version, or server-side resource constraints.
section_path: Measuring SMB throughput by using Robocopy > Procedure
